<!-- README.md -->

<div align="center">
  <img width="300" height="300" alt="image" src="https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/70f9a302-2f30-409c-b170-8f437391778a" />
  <h1>mnemo-warmup</h1>
</div>

<div align="center">

<b>Faster Java pod starts on Kubernetes, without GraalVM.</b>

<p>
Java services spend their first seconds loading and linking classes, on every deployment, scale-up and node move.
mnemo-warmup trains an AppCDS or Project Leyden AOT cache <b>once, inside your cluster</b>, and gives it to every replica of your
unchanged JVM application. A pod starts from the cache when it fits its launch exactly, and starts the ordinary way when it does not.
</p>

<a href="https://github.com/baokhang83/mnemo-warmup/actions/workflows/build.yml"><img alt="build" src="https://github.com/baokhang83/mnemo-warmup/actions/workflows/build.yml/badge.svg"></a>
<a href="https://baokhang83.github.io/mnemo-warmup/"><img alt="coverage" src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baokhang83/mnemo-warmup/refs/heads/gh-pages/badges/jacoco.svg"></a>
<a href="LICENSE"><img alt="License: Apache 2.0" src="https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Apache%202.0-blue.svg"></a>
<img alt="Status: alpha" src="https://img.shields.io/badge/status-alpha-yellow">
<img alt="Java 21+" src="https://img.shields.io/badge/java-21%2B-informational">

<p>
<a href="#try-the-example">Try the example</a> &middot;
<a href="#quick-start-in-three-steps">Quick start</a> &middot;
<a href="#measurements">Measurements</a> &middot;
<a href="docs/reference.md">Reference</a>
</p>

</div>

## Key benefits

- **Shorter JVM start-up, no rewrite.** Keep your JDK, your frameworks and your JAR. Pods start from a ready-made class cache instead of loading every class from scratch. Pod readiness improves where class loading dominates the start (Spring Boot: [-40%](#measurements)); [measure](docs/operations.md#measure-the-benefit) yours.
- **Three annotations, no source changes.** An injector adds the init containers, the launcher and the trainer to a plain Deployment, and you can preview every change first.
- **A cache problem never stops a pod.** A missing, outdated, damaged or unreachable cache means an ordinary start, and the log says why.
- **Set it up once.** When the image or JVM options change, the trainer builds a new cache by itself.
- **Fits what you already run.** An OCI registry you already have, Helm, and `java` stays PID 1. No controller, webhook or CRD. Works on distroless images.
- **AppCDS or the AOT cache**, chosen from your image's JDK (AppCDS on 21 and later, Leyden AOT on 25).

## How it works

<div align="center">
  <img src="docs/images/how-it-works.png" width="533" alt="How mnemo-warmup works: a Deployment with three annotations is rendered and injected; a trainer CronJob trains once per fingerprint and stores the archive in an OCI registry; a new pod's fetch init container verifies the digest, and the launcher starts Java with the cache flag if the archive fits the exact launch, or starts Java as before and logs why if it does not" />
</div>

- A **fingerprint** identifies what a cache is valid for: the JDK build, the classpath JAR contents and the JVM options.
- The **trainer** is a CronJob that runs your application image once per new fingerprint, stores the cache in the registry, and takes a Kubernetes Lease so only one trainer works at a time.
- Each **pod** gets its tools (two init containers, or a read-only `image` volume on clusters that support it) and starts through a small static launcher. When the image or JVM options change, a new fingerprint is trained.

> **Status: alpha.** Command-line options, annotations, chart values and the manifest format may still change. Validate both the benefit and the deployment behaviour with your own workload before you rely on it. [What has and has not been verified](docs/operations.md#known-limitations).

## Try the example

Run the bundled Spring Boot application through the whole annotated path on a throw-away [kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/) cluster, on a Temurin and on a distroless Java image:

```bash
git clone --depth 1 --branch v0.2.5 https://github.com/baokhang83/mnemo-warmup.git mnemo-warmup-src
cd mnemo-warmup-src
scripts/e2e-kind-inject.sh temurin     # needs docker, kind, kubectl, Helm 3, Java 21+ and Maven; several minutes
```

It previews and installs an annotated Deployment, shows it starting without a cache, trains one, restarts the pods onto it, changes a JVM option, corrupts the stored archive, stops the registry, and removes everything, checking at each step that the application still starts. See [`examples/`](examples/README.md).

## Quick start in three steps

**Before you start:** the CLI runs on your machine for the preview and as the Helm post-renderer. It needs Java 21 or newer and comes in the tools image (the same one the injected init containers use):

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/out --entrypoint cp ghcr.io/baokhang83/mnemo-warmup-tools:0.2.5 -r /opt/mnemo-warmup /out/
export PATH="$PWD/mnemo-warmup/bin:$PATH"
mnemo-warmup --version
```

Helm 3 calls an executable as the post-renderer. Save this as `mnemo-warmup-inject` and `chmod +x` it:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
exec mnemo-warmup inject "$@"
```

### Step 1: annotate the Deployment

Add three annotations to the Deployment's **pod template**, and give the container an explicit Java command (`java [options] -jar <jar> [args]`):

```yaml
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        warmup.mnemo.io/enabled: "true"
        warmup.mnemo.io/store: "oci://registry.example.com/team/my-app-warmup"
        warmup.mnemo.io/exit-mode: "spring-refresh"     # or http-probe, with warmup.mnemo.io/probe-url
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: registry.example.com/team/my-app:1.4.2
          command: ["java"]
          args: ["-Xmx512m", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]
```

The store is a repository for caches, not for your application image. [Every annotation and override](docs/configuration.md#annotations).

### Step 2: preview

```bash
helm template my-app ./my-chart --namespace my-namespace \
  | mnemo-warmup inject --namespace my-namespace --preview
```

The preview names the application container, image and JAR, the store, the trainer mode, and what the trainer copies from your workload (environment variable names, `envFrom` names, volumes and mounts, **never values**), then lists the Kubernetes fields it would add or change. The trainer starts your application with that configuration, so read it. A launch the injector cannot handle is reported here with the reason, and nothing is changed.

### Step 3: deploy

```bash
helm upgrade --install my-app ./my-chart --namespace my-namespace \
  --post-renderer ./mnemo-warmup-inject \
  --post-renderer-args=--namespace=my-namespace
```

The injector adds the install and fetch init containers, starts your application through the launcher, and adds a trainer CronJob with its ServiceAccount and Role. Your application's source does not change. With Helm 4, or without Helm, pipe `helm template` through `mnemo-warmup inject` and apply the result ([details](docs/offline-injector.md)).

> **Spring Boot:** the trainer and every pod must run the same JAR files, so extract the Spring Boot JAR when you build the image. [Preparing the image](docs/configuration.md#spring-boot), with a distroless example.

### Then: train and check that it works

The trainer runs every 10 minutes. To train now and check the result:

```bash
kubectl -n my-namespace get cronjob
kubectl -n my-namespace create job first-train --from=cronjob/<trainer-cronjob>
kubectl -n my-namespace wait --for=condition=complete job/first-train --timeout=15m
kubectl -n my-namespace logs job/first-train -c trainer                   # train: TRAINED ...
kubectl -n my-namespace rollout restart deployment/my-app
kubectl -n my-namespace logs <new-pod> -c mnemo-warmup-fetch               # Archive: ... (APP_CDS)
```

A selected archive shows the integration works. It does **not** show that pods became ready faster: [measure the whole start](docs/operations.md#measure-the-benefit).

## Registry authentication

The trainer needs read and write access to the archive repository, the pods read-only access. Use Docker-config Secrets (`warmup.mnemo.io/pull-secret`, `push-secret`) for registries with Basic or Bearer login. On **Amazon EKS**, pods can use IAM roles for service accounts to get an ECR login with no stored password. Both are in [registry authentication](docs/registry-auth.md) and the [EKS and ECR guide](docs/aws-workload-identity.md); the ECR path has not yet been verified on a live cluster.

## Minimal and distroless images

The injector supports Java images without `/bin/sh`, including distroless ones: every generated step runs a static launcher copied into the pod. It supports launches of the form `java [JVM options] -jar <jar> [arguments]`. The preview reports anything else with the reason. The bundled example is built and run on `gcr.io/distroless/java21-debian12` in the end-to-end test.

## Requirements

- Kubernetes with CronJobs and the Lease API; `Deployment` workloads.
- An application image with Java 21 or newer and a supported `java ... -jar ...` launch.
- An OCI registry reachable from the cluster, with the permissions above.
- The same JAR files in the trainer and in every pod.
- A workload whose startup can safely run once more in a separate trainer pod.

Details and what is not supported: [configuration](docs/configuration.md#requirements).

## Operational considerations

- **Training starts a real instance of your application.** Connections, migrations and scheduled jobs may run. Review the preview.
- **The first pods start uncached.** Training is asynchronous; later pods use the archive.
- **Caches use registry storage, and nothing deletes them.** Set a [retention policy](docs/archive-retention.md) on the archive repository.
- **Cache problems fall back; deployment problems do not.** A missing, damaged or unreachable archive means an ordinary start. A missing Secret, an unpullable image or a wrong command can still keep a pod from starting: [what can still stop a pod](docs/operations.md#what-can-still-stop-a-pod).

## Measurements

**Will it make my pods start faster?** It depends on what your app does while it starts. We measured three real applications (1 CPU, 1 GiB, 12 restarts each).

| Workload Profile | Pod start-to-Ready | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 🟢 **Spring Boot**: start-up is mostly loading classes and creating beans | **5 s → 3 s**<br>40% faster | **Worth it.** The JVM itself starts 41% faster. |
| 🟡 **Jenkins**: start-up is mostly the application running its own setup code (initializing plugins and configuration) | **4 s → 4 s**<br>no change | **Neutral.** The JVM starts 13% faster, the pod is ready at the same time. |
| 🔴 **SonarQube**: the container starts a small launcher, which starts three other JVMs that do the real work | **15 s → 17 s**<br>13% slower | **Not a fit yet.** The cache only reaches the launcher ([#77](https://github.com/baokhang83/mnemo-warmup/issues/77)). |

**The rule of thumb:** the more of your start-up is class loading (typical for Spring Boot and similar frameworks), the more you gain. If it is mostly your own initialization code, or a launcher that starts other JVMs, expect little or nothing.

> **Use the `image` volume where your cluster supports it.** The green and yellow rows deliver the tools as a Kubernetes [`image` volume](docs/configuration.md#tools-delivery-init-containers-or-an-image-volume), which needs no init containers. With init containers the Spring Boot pod is ready in 5 s either way (the init containers cost what the cache saves), and Jenkins is 1 s slower. The red row used init containers.

Numbers are medians and pod times have a one-second resolution: read the direction, not the decimals. Measure your own app with `mnemo-warmup bench --jar app.jar` or [the cluster method](docs/operations.md#measure-the-benefit). Method, raw data and limits: [benchmarks](benchmarks/README.md). More studies (JDK 21 vs 25, app size, scale-out, alternatives) are planned for the [0.3.0 beta](https://github.com/baokhang83/mnemo-warmup/milestone/3).

## Disable or remove it

Remove the `warmup.mnemo.io/*` annotations (or set `enabled` to `"false"`) and redeploy through the injector. The next render has your original command and no init containers, and Helm removes the generated trainer resources. Archives stay in the registry until your retention policy removes them. [Details](docs/operations.md#disable-or-remove-it).

## Other ways in

The explicit Helm-subchart setup (you wire the helpers into your own templates; needs `/bin/sh` in the image) is in [docs/helm-chart.md](docs/helm-chart.md).

## Building from source

Requirements: JDK 21+ and Maven 3.9+. The code compiles with `--release 21` and is tested
on JDK 25.

```bash
mvn verify
java -jar warmup-cli/target/mnemo-warmup.jar --version
java -jar warmup-cli/target/mnemo-warmup.jar build --help
```

The build produces a self-contained `warmup-cli/target/mnemo-warmup.jar`; the examples above
call it as `mnemo-warmup`.

## Contributing

The project is at a very early stage and the design is still moving. Issues and
discussion about the open decisions in the plan are the most useful contribution right
now.

<!-- docs/configuration.md -->

# Configuration and requirements

How the annotation path decides what to change, what you can override, and what your application and cluster need. For the command-line options of `build`, `push`, `fetch` and the rest, see the [reference](reference.md). For the generated resources and the preview output, see the [offline injector guide](offline-injector.md).

## Requirements

- **Kubernetes** with `batch/v1` CronJobs (1.21 or newer) and the `coordination.k8s.io/v1` Lease API. The injector handles `Deployment` resources only.
- **Application image:** Java **21 or newer** (the trainer fails visibly without it; `fetch` and start fall back to an ordinary start). With the injector the image needs no shell, so distroless Java images work. The Helm-chart setup does need `/bin/sh` ([chart guide](helm-chart.md)).
- **Launch command:** an explicit `java [JVM options] -jar <jar> [arguments]` in the container's `command` and `args`. Launches with `-cp` and a main class are not supported by the injector.
- **JARs fixed at build time:** the trainer and every pod must run the same files. For Spring Boot 3.3 or newer, extract the JAR when you build the image ([below](#spring-boot)); another executable JAR needs its dependencies listed in its `Class-Path`.
- **An OCI registry** reachable from the cluster, for archives: [authentication](registry-auth.md) and storage are covered there. Archives can reach hundreds of MB, so check the registry's blob-size limit, and keep tag immutability off for the archive repository.
- **A workload whose startup can run once more, for real, in a separate trainer pod** ([operations](operations.md#what-it-costs)).

## Annotations

Set these on the Deployment's **pod template** (`spec.template.metadata.annotations`). Values are strings, so quote `"true"`.

| Annotation | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `warmup.mnemo.io/enabled` | yes | `"true"` turns adoption on. `"false"` (or leaving the annotations out) leaves the workload untouched and restores fields the injector owns on an already-injected stream. |
| `warmup.mnemo.io/store` | yes | The archive repository, `oci://host[:port]/path`. Not your application image repository. |
| `warmup.mnemo.io/exit-mode` | yes | How the trainer knows startup is done: `spring-refresh` (Spring Boot: the context has refreshed) or `http-probe` (any application: an HTTP URL answers). |
| `warmup.mnemo.io/probe-url` | with `http-probe` only | An HTTP URL reachable from the trainer pod. Not allowed with `spring-refresh`. |
| `warmup.mnemo.io/container` | if the pod has several containers | The name of the application container. |
| `warmup.mnemo.io/command` | no | A complete JSON string array for the launch, for an image whose Java command comes from `ENTRYPOINT`, for example `["java","-jar","/app/app.jar"]`. Replaces `command` plus `args` for discovery only. |
| `warmup.mnemo.io/pull-secret` | no | Name of a `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` Secret in the workload's namespace with **pull** access to the archive repository. [Details](registry-auth.md#docker-config-secrets). |
| `warmup.mnemo.io/push-secret` | no | The same with **push** access, used by the trainer. |
| `warmup.mnemo.io/plain-http` | no | `"true"` talks plain HTTP to the registry. Local registries and tests only. |
| `warmup.mnemo.io/tools-delivery` | no | How the tools reach the pod: `init-container` (the default, described below) or `image-volume`, which leaves the pod with **no init containers** on the start path. See [Tools delivery](#tools-delivery-init-containers-or-an-image-volume). It cannot be combined with `pull-secret`. |

**Three annotations are required today, not two:** `enabled`, `store` and `exit-mode`. The injector stops with `missing warmup.mnemo.io/exit-mode` otherwise, because it does not guess how your application signals that it has started.

The injector also needs a namespace for the trainer resources. If your rendered Deployment has no `metadata.namespace` (Helm output usually has none), pass `--namespace` ([guide](offline-injector.md)).

## How the launch command is read

The selected container must have an explicit `command` and optional `args` that form:

```text
java [JVM options] -jar <jar> [application arguments]
```

- The first word must be `java` or end in `/java`.
- Everything between `java` and `-jar` is a JVM option. Each must start with `-`. `-cp`, `--class-path`, `-classpath` and `@argfiles` are refused.
- The word after `-jar` is the JAR path. The injector gives the JVM options to `fetch` and to the trainer, so **a changed JVM option is a new fingerprint**: new pods start without an archive until the trainer has trained one for the new options, and rolling back finds the old archive again.
- Anything else is reported by the preview with the reason, and nothing is changed. Use `warmup.mnemo.io/command` when the image supplies the Java command.

## Spring Boot

An archive remembers the JAR files it was trained on, so the trainer and every pod must run identical files at identical paths. Extract the Spring Boot JAR when you build the image:

```dockerfile
RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar target/app.jar extract --destination /out
...
COPY --from=build /out /app
```

and run `java -jar /app/app.jar` (so the annotation path sees `-jar /app/app.jar`). The trainer starts the application for real and stops it once the Spring context has refreshed (`exit-mode: spring-refresh`). Complete, buildable examples: [`examples/spring-boot/Dockerfile`](../examples/spring-boot/Dockerfile) (Temurin) and [`examples/spring-boot/Dockerfile.distroless`](../examples/spring-boot/Dockerfile.distroless) (no shell).

The image's JDK decides the cache type: AppCDS on JDK 21 and later, the Leyden AOT cache on JDK 25. The annotation path was run end to end on JDK 21 (AppCDS) only; the Helm-chart path covers both.

## What the injector adds

For each opted-in Deployment, by default: two init containers (`mnemo-warmup-install` copies the launcher and tools from the tools image; `mnemo-warmup-fetch` runs `fetch` in your application's image), a changed application command that starts `java` through the launcher so it is still PID 1, shared `emptyDir` volumes, and a trainer **CronJob** with its ServiceAccount, Role (leases only) and RoleBinding. The CronJob runs every 10 minutes, does not overlap runs and stops a run after one hour; these values are not configurable in this release.

### Tools delivery: init containers or an image volume

By default (`init-container`) two init containers run before every start, one after the other: the first copies the tools out of the tools image, the second fetches the archive. Their own work takes well under a second, but the kubelet starts containers one at a time and each costs a start-up, so on the benchmark clusters they delayed the application's start by about 1.75 s ([ADR 0012](adr/0012-tools-as-an-image-volume.md)).

`warmup.mnemo.io/tools-delivery: "image-volume"` removes both:

- the tools image is mounted as a read-only **image volume**, so nothing has to copy it, and the tools are at `/mnemo-tools/opt/mnemo-warmup/` in the pod;
- the launcher does the fetch itself, in your application container's entrypoint, and then replaces itself with `java` as before (`mnemo-launcher exec <fetch options> -- java ...`), so the JVM is still PID 1;
- the trainer pod uses the same volume and has no init container either;
- the application container mounts the cache read-write (it writes the fetched archive) and a scratch volume, and the fetch runs with the application's own environment, security context and resource limits. The native fetch is small; the Java fallback (a first deploy, an ECR registry, a Spring Boot fat JAR) runs a JVM inside the container briefly, so leave room for it in a tight memory limit.

What it needs and what it costs:

- **A cluster and container runtime that support image volumes** (Kubernetes 1.33 or later, where the feature is beta, and containerd 2.1 or later or CRI-O 1.31 or later; check yours). On a cluster without them a pod with the volume **does not start**. That is a deployment failure, like a missing Secret, not a cache failure, and it is why the mode is opt-in. It was verified on kind with Kubernetes 1.36.1 and containerd 2.3.1.
- **No `pull-secret`.** The fetch runs in the application container, so the Secret would be readable by the application's code. The injector stops with a message when the two are combined. Anonymous registries and registries reached through workload identity work. `push-secret` belongs to the trainer and is fine.
- The fetch's log lines appear in the application container's log, not in a container of their own.

To go back, remove the annotation or set it to `init-container` and render again: the injector records the mode it applied and restores the original Deployment either way.

The trainer copies what the application needs to start: environment variables and `envFrom` references, volumes and mounts, the image pull policy and security context, image pull secrets, node selector, tolerations and affinity. The preview lists these by **name only**; review it, because the trainer starts your application with that configuration.

## Not supported in this release

- Workloads other than `Deployment`; launches with `-cp` and a main class; JVM options that start with `@` (argument files).
- Per-workload trainer schedule, deadline or resources.
- Registry login through credential helpers, GKE and AKS workload identity, and EKS Pod Identity ([registry authentication](registry-auth.md)).
- Helm 4 post-renderer plugins: the post-renderer here is a script path, which Helm 3 accepts ([guide](offline-injector.md)).


---

<!-- docs/operations.md -->

# Operating mnemo-warmup

What it costs, how to check that it works, what can and cannot stop a pod, and how to bound storage and remove it. Setup is in the [README](../README.md) and [configuration](configuration.md).

## What it costs

- **Training runs a real instance of your application**, once per new fingerprint (for Spring Boot until the context has refreshed). Whatever startup does (connections, migrations, background jobs, calls to other services) also happens in the trainer pod. The trainer copies your environment, `envFrom`, volumes and mounts; review the [preview](offline-injector.md) and give it a safe configuration.
- **Pods do extra work before they are ready:** two init containers, the archive download, and hashing the classpath JARs and the archive. Larger classpaths and archives cost more. The saving only counts if it is larger than this.
- **One archive per fingerprint** (per image, JDK and JVM options) is stored in your registry and is never deleted by this tool. See [retention](#retention).
- **The first pods start uncached.** Training is asynchronous: the trainer runs on its schedule (every 10 minutes) after you deploy, and only pods that start after it has finished can use the archive.

## Check that it works

After the trainer has finished (`kubectl get jobs`; its log says `train: TRAINED` or `ALREADY_STORED`), start new pods and read what they did:

```bash
kubectl -n NS rollout restart deployment/my-app
kubectl -n NS logs POD -c mnemo-warmup-fetch    # Archive: ... (APP_CDS)   or   (LEYDEN_AOT) on JDK 25
kubectl -n NS logs POD -c app | grep "run:"     # run: using APP_CDS archive ...
```

A trained, selected archive shows the integration works. It does **not** show that pods became ready faster.

## Measure the benefit

Compare **pod creation to Ready** with and without the cache over several restarts, including the init containers:

```bash
kubectl -n NS get pods -l app=my-app -o json | jq -r '.items[] | [.metadata.name,
  (((.status.conditions[]|select(.type=="Ready").lastTransitionTime|fromdate) - (.metadata.creationTimestamp|fromdate)))] | @tsv'
```

Pod condition times have a resolution of one second. For the JVM's own start-up figure, read the application log ("Started ... in N seconds") or run `mnemo-warmup bench --jar app.jar`, which compares no cache, AppCDS and AOT locally ([reference](reference.md#measure-the-savings-bench)).

For scale, not as a prediction: on a Spring Boot application with 69 JARs and a 1 CPU / 1 GiB limit (arm64 kind cluster), the JVM-reported start was a median 3.19 s without and 1.89 s with the archive. Pod start-to-Ready was 5 s without mnemo-warmup, 5 s with the archive and init containers, and 3 s with the tools delivered as an `image` volume. Jenkins gained 0.3 s of JVM start and was at parity in pod readiness; SonarQube, whose container starts a coordinator for three more JVMs, gained nothing. The method, raw data, per-phase breakdown and limits are in [benchmarks](../benchmarks/README.md). On the small bundled example the JVM start fell from 0.48 s to 0.31 s and pod start-to-Ready stayed at 2 to 3 s ([details](offline-injector.md#verification)). Measure your own application.

## What can still stop a pod

Failures **looking up or validating** the archive never stop a pod; it starts the ordinary way and its log says why.

| Situation | What you see |
|---|---|
| No archive yet (first deploy) | `fetch`: "No usable archive"; `run`: "no archive was fetched" |
| A JVM option differs from when the archive was trained | a new fingerprint: `fetch` finds none and the trainer trains one on its next run |
| New image or JARs | a new fingerprint, the same |
| Registry unreachable or login refused | `fetch` logs the reason and exits 0; the pod becomes Ready after `fetch` gives up (about 15 s with an unreachable registry in the end-to-end run) |
| Stored archive damaged | rejected by the digest check; the pod starts uncached |
| The image has no Java, or Java older than 21 | the launcher skips the tool and your app starts as before |

**Deployment failures are not covered**, because the pod cannot get as far as running the tool:

- a `pull-secret` or `push-secret` that does not exist in the namespace;
- the tools image or the application image cannot be pulled;
- with the Helm chart, an application image without `/bin/sh`;
- an application command that is wrong in the first place;
- with `tools-delivery: image-volume` ([ADR 0012](adr/0012-tools-as-an-image-volume.md)), a cluster or container runtime that does not support image volumes: the pod stays in `ContainerCreating` and its events say why. Remove the annotation (or set it to `init-container`) to go back.

Pass `--strict` to `fetch` only if you want a missing archive to fail the pod. Do not do this in production start paths.

## Retention

Archives accumulate: one per fingerprint, hundreds of MB each, and nothing here deletes them. Bound the growth with your registry's lifecycle policy, scoped to a dedicated archive repository and to `fp-` tags. [Archive retention](archive-retention.md) explains what a deletion costs (a cache miss and one re-training run, not an outage), why a time-to-live rule does not protect running versions, and includes a reviewable Amazon ECR policy.

## Disable or remove it

To stop using the cache for a workload, remove the `warmup.mnemo.io/*` annotations (or set `enabled` to `"false"`) and redeploy through the injector. The next render has the original command, no init containers or volumes, and, with Helm, Helm removes the generated CronJob, ServiceAccount, Role and RoleBinding. With a plain `kubectl apply` of the injected output, delete the generated resources yourself: `kubectl -n NS delete cronjob,serviceaccount,role,rolebinding -l warmup.mnemo.io/owner=my-app`.

Archives stay in the registry until your retention policy or an operator removes them. Leases left behind expire on their own (`kubectl -n NS get lease | grep mnemo-warmup`).

## Known limitations

- **Trainer service account and IRSA.** The injector generates the trainer's ServiceAccount and has no annotation for it, so the EKS role annotation for the push role must be added by your own patch after rendering. The application's service account is yours and carries the pull role. See [registry authentication](registry-auth.md#eks-and-ecr).
- **Trainer schedule, deadline and resources** are fixed (every 10 minutes, one hour, none set).
- **Verified on:** kind with Helm 3, a plain-HTTP registry, JDK 21 (AppCDS), a Temurin and a distroless Java 21 image, arm64 locally; amd64 and arm64 in CI once that job has run. **Not verified:** a live EKS and ECR, Helm 4, JDK 25 through the injector, multi-container pods.
- Alpha: command-line options, annotations and the manifest format may still change.


---

<!-- docs/offline-injector.md -->

# Offline workload injector

The injector reads a complete rendered Kubernetes YAML stream from standard input. It does not contact the cluster. It emits transformed manifests on standard output and diagnostics on standard error. It requires Helm or another deployer to apply and remove the resulting resources.

Annotate the Deployment pod template:

```yaml
warmup.mnemo.io/enabled: "true"
warmup.mnemo.io/store: "oci://registry.example.com/team/app-warmup"
warmup.mnemo.io/exit-mode: "spring-refresh"
```

For `http-probe`, set `warmup.mnemo.io/probe-url` to an HTTP URL reachable from the trainer pod. Select one container with `warmup.mnemo.io/container` if the pod has more than one. The selected container must have an explicit `command` and optional `args` forming `java [options] -jar <jar> [args]`. For an image-supplied entrypoint, supply a complete JSON string array through `warmup.mnemo.io/command`.

For a private archive registry, `warmup.mnemo.io/pull-secret` and `warmup.mnemo.io/push-secret` name separate `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` Secrets in the workload namespace. Image-pull credentials do not automatically grant access to the archive store. An absent Secret prevents a pod that mounts it from starting. The trainer runs the application with its configuration; review startup side effects and copied mounts before use.

```sh
helm template my-app ./my-chart --namespace my-namespace \
  | mnemo-warmup inject --namespace my-namespace --preview

helm upgrade --install my-app ./my-chart --namespace my-namespace \
  --post-renderer ./scripts/mnemo-warmup-inject \
  --post-renderer-args=--namespace=my-namespace
```

The adapter requires `mnemo-warmup` on `PATH`. **Helm version:** this form (`--post-renderer` with a path to an executable) is Helm 3's interface. Helm's reference for 4.3.1 describes `--post-renderer` as taking *the name of a post-renderer plugin* (and lists `--post-renderer-args`), so on Helm 4 a script path is not expected to work; a plugin is needed, and this repository does not ship one yet. This has not been tested on Helm 4. Until then, with Helm 4 render and inject in a pipeline (`helm template ... | mnemo-warmup inject --namespace ... | kubectl apply -f -`, or commit the result for GitOps), keeping in mind that resources applied that way are not tracked as a Helm release, so removal needs your deployer to prune them. Preview prints workload details and changed paths without field values. Helm output contains the complete transformed stream; an error returns nonzero without emitting a partial stream. If the rendered Deployment does not specify `metadata.namespace`, pass `--namespace` so trainer resources use the release namespace.

**Tools image.** The generated `mnemo-warmup-install` init containers run `/opt/mnemo-warmup/bin/mnemo-launcher install /mnemo-tools` in `ghcr.io/baokhang83/mnemo-warmup-tools:<version>`, where `<version>` is the release version of the `mnemo-warmup` that runs the injector (the CLI is shipped in that same image). A development build has no release version and stops with a message asking for `--tools-image <image>`; pass it explicitly (it is also how to point at a private mirror), for example `--post-renderer-args=--tools-image=registry.example.com/mirror/mnemo-warmup-tools:0.2.5`. A stream with no opted-in workload never needs it.

**Without init containers.** Add `warmup.mnemo.io/tools-delivery: "image-volume"` to mount the tools image as an image volume and let the launcher fetch inside the application container, so the pod has no init containers on the start path. It needs a cluster that supports image volumes, and cannot be combined with `pull-secret`; the [annotation reference](configuration.md#tools-delivery-init-containers-or-an-image-volume) and [ADR 0012](adr/0012-tools-as-an-image-volume.md) have the details. The preview shows `tools-delivery=` for each workload. Switching between the two modes, in either direction, is a re-render: the injector first restores the Deployment from what it recorded, then applies the mode now asked for.

**What the preview lists.** For each opted-in workload: container, image, JAR, store, trainer mode and tools image, then what the trainer and fetch containers copy from the workload, **by name only** (environment variable names, `envFrom` Secret/ConfigMap names, volume names and their kind, mount paths) and the archive credential Secret names. It never prints a value. Review that list: the trainer starts the application for real with that configuration.

**Generated trainer.** One CronJob (`*/10 * * * *`, `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid`, 3600 s deadline), ServiceAccount, Role (`get`, `create`, `update`, `delete` on `leases` only) and RoleBinding per workload, named after the Deployment with a short hash suffix. These settings are not configurable yet. Deployment names longer than 63 characters are rejected, because the Deployment name is used as a label value on the generated resources.

Disable by removing the opt-in annotation from the source Deployment and rerendering. Helm owns removal of generated resources. For an already-injected stream, set the annotation to `"false"`; the injector restores fields it owns and rejects changes to managed fields. It does not delete archives or external Secrets. Repeated transformation must not accumulate warmup resources.

Current limitations: this injector requires an explicit Java launch, a registry URL and a trainer mode. It does not inspect image metadata or infer readiness probes. Every generated container runs the static `mnemo-launcher`, so the application image needs no shell and distroless images work; it does need Java 21 or newer (the trainer fails visibly without it, the fetch and start steps fall back to an ordinary start). Details and differences from the shell launcher, such as `fetch --strict` and non-ASCII arguments, are in [the reference](reference.md#shell-free-distroless-application-images). Inspect the preview and generated trainer configuration before deploying. Kubernetes image, Secret and volume errors can still block a pod even though cache lookup and validation failures fall back to an ordinary start.

## Verification

`scripts/e2e-kind-inject.sh` runs the annotated path on a real kind cluster with Helm 3 and the injector as a post-renderer, using a plain Deployment with three annotations (`examples/annotated-app`) and a local registry as the archive store. It runs twice, once with an `eclipse-temurin` JRE image (has a shell) and once with `gcr.io/distroless/java21-debian12` (no shell). For each image it checks:

- **Preview:** names the workload, store and copied environment variable names; prints no value.
- **First start:** the application becomes Ready without an archive, `fetch` logs that it found none and exits 0, and the original `java` options, `-jar` and JAR follow the launcher in the container arguments. On the temurin image `java` is PID 1.
- **Asynchronous training:** a separate Job trains and uploads while the application stays Ready; a second Job finds the entry and does not train; the Lease is released.
- **Cache hit:** after a pod restart `fetch` finds the archive and the application's own class loads from it. Deleting the pod ends it in about a second, so SIGTERM reaches `java`.
- **Workload update and rollback:** a changed JVM option is a new fingerprint, because the injector passes the options to `fetch` and the trainer. The updated pod starts uncached with the reason logged, the trainer trains an archive for the new options, and rolling back finds the original archive again.
- **Invalid cache:** 4 KiB of the stored archive are overwritten with random bytes (same size). `fetch` rejects it by digest and the pod starts uncached and Ready. The test fails if the corruption step does not actually change the blob.
- **Registry failure:** with the registry stopped, the pod becomes Ready about 14 to 15 seconds after the pod is deleted (the time `fetch` takes to give up); once the registry is back, new pods use the archive again.
- **Removal:** with `warmup.enabled=false` the Deployment has its original command and no init containers or volumes, and Helm prunes the generated CronJob, ServiceAccount, Role and RoleBinding. This holds for both tools-delivery modes.
- **Image-volume mode:** the same scenarios run with `warmup.toolsDelivery=image-volume`: the pod has no init containers, the archive is fetched and used, the corrupted archive is rejected, the stopped registry does not stop the pod, and removal restores the Deployment.

```sh
scripts/e2e-kind-inject.sh                 # both images; needs docker, kind, kubectl, Helm 3, Java 21 and network access
scripts/e2e-kind-inject.sh distroless      # one image
REPEATS=5 KEEP=1 scripts/e2e-kind-inject.sh
```

**Start-to-Ready.** The script reports the pod's start-to-Ready time from its own condition timestamps (creation to Ready, and creation to the end of the init containers), `REPEATS` times with and without an archive, and the "Started ... in N seconds" figure that Spring prints. It reports and never fails on speed. On one run on an arm64 kind cluster (Docker Desktop on macOS), the example application started in a median 0.48 s without an archive and 0.31 s with one on both images. Pod conditions have a resolution of one second and the example application is very small, so the pod start-to-Ready times were 2 to 3 seconds both with and without an archive and the difference is not visible there. These numbers do not predict savings for a large application; use `mnemo-warmup bench` on your own JAR.

**Where it runs.** The `e2e` GitHub Actions workflow has a `kind-inject` job for linux/amd64 (`ubuntu-latest`) and linux/arm64 (`ubuntu-24.04-arm`). At the time of writing this was run locally on arm64 only; the CI job itself has not yet run. Treat everything below as unverified until it has.

**Not verified:**

- linux/amd64, until the CI job has run, and any architecture the cluster does not run natively;
- a real cloud registry and EKS/ECR workload identity: the script uses an unauthenticated plain-HTTP registry on the kind network (the ECR path is covered by unit tests with local fakes and by [the setup guide](aws-workload-identity.md) checklist);
- Helm 4 (see above), GitOps tools that apply rendered output, and clusters other than kind;
- JDK 25 (AOT) through the injector: the script uses JDK 21 (AppCDS), and `scripts/e2e-kind.sh` covers both JDKs through the chart;
- a Deployment with several containers, probes with a startup probe, or applications that need Secrets or volumes at start-up;
- whether the trainer repairs a stored archive whose bytes were corrupted without changing its size (the script shows that `fetch` rejects it, not what the trainer does next).



---

<!-- docs/reference.md -->

# mnemo-warmup reference

The details behind the [README](../README.md): the problem, the cache types, every command and its options, the container
image, the Helm chart and trainer, the manifest and fingerprint, and the current limits. For setting it up on a cluster, start
with the README.

## Why

The JVM can start faster when it reuses an archive of already-loaded and linked classes: **AppCDS** (JDK 13+) and
**Project Leyden's AOT cache** (JDK 24+; single-step creation since JDK 25, JEP 514). How much faster depends on the
application; this project's own (small) measurements are in the README. Using them in practice is awkward, because:

1. **Training is a ceremony.** You unpack the JAR, run the app, exercise it, and stop it
   cleanly so the archive is written.
2. **Archives are fragile.** They are bound to the exact JDK build, classpath and JVM flags.
   A mismatch silently disables the archive or fails startup.
3. **CI is the wrong place to train.** Real config, secrets and dependencies live in the
   cluster, not in the build.
4. **Nobody measures it.** There is no routine way to see what an archive actually saves.

## Cache types

AppCDS and the AOT cache are alternatives: the JVM is given one archive per run
(`-XX:SharedArchiveFile` or `-XX:AOTCache`). The AOT cache builds on the CDS machinery and
stores more.

| JDK | AppCDS (`.jsa`) | AOT cache (`.aot`) |
|-----|-----------------|--------------------|
| 21-23 | Supported | Not available |
| 24 | Supported | Needs a two-step flow; not supported yet |
| 25+ | Supported (fallback) | **Preferred**, single step (`-XX:AOTCacheOutput`) |

`cacheType: auto` (the default) chooses AOT on JDK 25+ and AppCDS otherwise. You can also
force `appcds` or `aot`.

## Usage

Build the CLI (see [Building from source](../README.md#building-from-source)), then train an archive:

```bash
# Spring Boot 3.3+ fat JAR: extract it, then let Spring end the run after the context refresh
mnemo-warmup build --jar app.jar

# Any framework: wait for a health endpoint, send some warmup traffic, then stop the app
mnemo-warmup build --jar app.jar --exit-mode http-probe \
    --url http://localhost:8080/actuator/health \
    --warmup-url /api/items --warmup-url /api/orders

# Train for a different JDK than the one running the tool, and force a cache type
mnemo-warmup build --jar app.jar --java-home /opt/jdk-21 --cache-type appcds
```

The archive is written to `<work-dir>/app.aot` or `<work-dir>/app.jsa` (default work
directory `.mnemo-warmup`), next to a `mnemo-warmup.manifest.json` (see below). Run the application later with the same JDK, JAR and flags and
pass `-XX:AOTCache=<file>` (AOT) or `-XX:SharedArchiveFile=<file>` (AppCDS).

| Option | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `--jar` | Application JAR. Spring Boot 3.3+ fat JARs are extracted with `-Djarmode=tools`; other executable JARs are used as they are. |
| `--java-home` | JDK of the target app. Defaults to `$JAVA_HOME`, then the JDK running the tool. |
| `--cache-type` | `auto` (default), `appcds` or `aot`. `auto` picks AOT on JDK 25+, AppCDS otherwise. |
| `--exit-mode` | `spring-refresh` (default) or `http-probe`. |
| `--url` | `http-probe`: endpoint that must return 2xx. Required for that mode. |
| `--warmup-url` | `http-probe`: GET request after the probe succeeds (repeatable; absolute URL or path). |
| `--warmup-script` | `http-probe`: program run after the warmup requests; gets the base URL, must exit 0. |
| `--poll-interval-millis` | `http-probe`: pause between probes (default 500). |
| `--timeout-seconds` | How long the app may take to become ready (default 300). |
| `--jvm-arg` | JVM option for the training run, e.g. `--jvm-arg=-Xmx512m` (repeatable). Use the options the app will run with. |
| `--image-digest` | Container image digest to record in the fingerprint. |
| `--work-dir` | Where files are written (default `.mnemo-warmup`). |

Exit codes: `0` success, `1` training failed (the message includes the app's last log
lines), `2` invalid input. A failed run never leaves an archive behind.

**Exit modes.** `spring-refresh` passes `-Dspring.context.exit=onRefresh`, so only the
startup path is trained. `http-probe` also trains the classes used while serving the
warmup requests you send, and works for any framework.

### Measure the savings: `bench`

```bash
mnemo-warmup bench --jar app.jar --runs 3
```

Starts the app with no archive, with AppCDS and (on JDK 25+) with AOT, in fresh JVMs, discards a
warm-up start and prints a Markdown table of median cold-start times. It takes the same application
options as `build`, plus `--runs` (timed starts per variant, default 3) and `--warmups` (default 1).

### Share the archive: `push`, `fetch`

```bash
# trainer: after `build`, upload the archive and manifest (tag = fp-<fingerprint hex>)
mnemo-warmup push --store oci://registry.example.com/team/warmup --registry-auth ~/.docker/config.json

# every pod, as an init container: look up, verify and write the archive
mnemo-warmup fetch --jar /app/app.jar --jvm-arg=-Xmx512m --image-digest sha256:... \
    --store oci://registry.example.com/team/warmup --out /mnemo-cache
```

`fetch` computes the live fingerprint the same way `build` does, so give it the same `--jar`,
`--jvm-arg` and `--image-digest` as the training run. With `--cache-type auto` it looks for an AOT
archive first (JDK 25+) and then AppCDS. A hit writes the archive, its manifest and a one-line
`mnemo-warmup.flags` file (for example `-XX:SharedArchiveFile=/mnemo-cache/app.jsa`) to `--out`.

| Option | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `--store` | `oci://host[:port]/repository`. Archives are OCI artifacts tagged `fp-<hex>`. |
| `--registry-auth` | Docker-config style JSON (a mounted `dockerconfigjson` Secret). `push` needs push scope, `fetch` pull scope. Defaults to `$MNEMO_WARMUP_REGISTRY_AUTH`, then anonymous. Basic and Bearer-token auth are supported. For an Amazon ECR registry on EKS with no file entry, the pod's IRSA identity is used ([setup](aws-workload-identity.md)); credential helpers, GKE and AKS are not supported yet. |
| `--plain-http` | Use http instead of https (local registries only). |
| `--out` | `fetch`: output directory (default `.mnemo-warmup/cache`). |
| `--cache-type` | `fetch`: `auto` (default), `appcds` or `aot`. |
| `--store-timeout-seconds` | `fetch`: per request and download stall (default 120). |
| `--strict` | `fetch`: exit 1 on a store problem and 2 on bad arguments, for CI. |

**`fetch` exits 0 by default**, whatever goes wrong (unreachable registry, bad login, corrupt
download, bad options). An init container that exits non-zero keeps the pod from starting, so the
failure is logged and any old flags file is removed instead. `push` uses exit codes normally:
`0` success, `1` store failure, `2` invalid input (including an archive that does not match its manifest).

### Start the app: `run`

```bash
# prints the final command; the wrapper script then execs it, so java is PID 1
mnemo-warmup run --print --cache-dir /mnemo-cache -- java -Xmx512m -jar /app/app.jar
```

`run` rebuilds the description of this exact launch and compares it with the manifest `fetch`
stored. Only if the JDK build, JVM options, classpath content, JAR modification times and the
directory the app was trained from all agree, it inserts `-XX:SharedArchiveFile=` or
`-XX:AOTCache=` right after `java`. Otherwise it starts the command exactly as given and logs why
(for example `-Xmx512m` against `-Xmx1g`). Only `java [options] -jar <jar> [args]` launches are
supported; anything else is left unchanged.

In a Dockerfile, use [`scripts/mnemo-warmup-exec`](../scripts/mnemo-warmup-exec) as the entrypoint:

```dockerfile
# Extract a Spring Boot fat JAR at build time, so training and running use the same files.
RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --destination /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/opt/mnemo-warmup/mnemo-warmup-exec"]
CMD ["java", "-Xmx512m", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]
```

The script runs `mnemo-warmup run --print` and then `exec`s the result, so the JVM replaces the
shell as PID 1 and receives Kubernetes' SIGTERM directly with no extra process. If `mnemo-warmup`
is missing or fails, it execs your original command. Images without `/bin/sh` can use
`mnemo-warmup run --spawn -- java ...` instead: it starts the command as a child process,
forwards SIGTERM, waits for it (up to `--stop-timeout-seconds`, default 25) and returns its exit
code, but keeps a second JVM resident.

Why extraction at build time: the JVM silently ignores an archive when a classpath JAR's size,
modification time or path differs from training. Run the same extracted files, at the same path,
in the trainer and in the app. If a Spring Boot fat JAR is launched directly, `run` says so and
starts it plain. See [ADR 0003](adr/0003-run-exec-model-and-layout.md).

`run` options: `--cache-dir` (default `$MNEMO_WARMUP_CACHE_DIR`, then `.mnemo-warmup/cache`),
`--image-digest` (default `$MNEMO_WARMUP_IMAGE_DIGEST`), `--print`, `--format shell|nul` (with `--print`:
one shell-quoted line for `eval`, the default, or each argument followed by a NUL byte for the native
launcher), `--spawn`, `--stop-timeout-seconds`.

## Container image

The tool has to run **inside your application image**, because an archive is only valid for that
image's JDK build, JAR files, paths and modification times. So the published image
`ghcr.io/baokhang83/mnemo-warmup-tools:<version>` (about 7 MB, amd64 and arm64) contains no JDK; it only
carries `/opt/mnemo-warmup/mnemo-warmup.jar`, the shell scripts `bin/mnemo-warmup` (launcher) and
`bin/mnemo-warmup-exec` (exec wrapper), and the static native launcher `bin/mnemo-launcher` for images
without a shell. Your application image needs Java 21 or newer.

Bake it into your image:

```dockerfile
COPY --from=ghcr.io/baokhang83/mnemo-warmup-tools:0.2.5 /opt/mnemo-warmup /opt/mnemo-warmup
ENTRYPOINT ["/opt/mnemo-warmup/bin/mnemo-warmup-exec"]
CMD ["java", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]
```

or copy it at deploy time with an init container (what the Helm chart does):

```yaml
initContainers:
  - name: mnemo-warmup-install
    image: ghcr.io/baokhang83/mnemo-warmup-tools:0.2.5
    command: ["cp", "-R", "/opt/mnemo-warmup/.", "/mnemo-tools/"]
    volumeMounts: [{ name: mnemo-tools, mountPath: /mnemo-tools }]
  - name: mnemo-warmup-fetch
    image: my-app:1.0            # the application image itself
    command: ["/mnemo-tools/bin/mnemo-warmup", "fetch", "--jar", "/app/app.jar",
              "--store", "oci://registry.example.com/team/warmup", "--out", "/mnemo-cache"]
    volumeMounts: [{ name: mnemo-tools, mountPath: /mnemo-tools }, { name: mnemo-cache, mountPath: /mnemo-cache }]
```

If the image has no Java, or one older than 21, the shell launcher makes `fetch` skip itself with exit 0 and
`run` start your original command unchanged, so the pod still starts. That safety net needs `/bin/sh`.
Build it locally with
`docker build -f image/Dockerfile -t mnemo-warmup-tools .`, and check the whole chain in Docker with
`scripts/verify-image.sh` (a local registry, JDK 21 with AppCDS and JDK 25 with AOT).
See [ADR 0004](adr/0004-tools-image.md).

### Shell-free (distroless) application images

`bin/mnemo-launcher` is a static Go program (no libc, no shell; linux/amd64 and linux/arm64) that replaces
the three shell steps. The offline injector uses it for every container it generates; the Helm chart still
uses the shell scripts.

| Command | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `mnemo-launcher install <dir>` | Copies the tools into `<dir>` (what `cp -R` did). Run it from the tools image, which still has the files at `/opt/mnemo-warmup`. |
| `mnemo-launcher fetch <options>` | Runs `java -jar mnemo-warmup.jar fetch <options>`. A missing `java` or a failing jar is logged and exits 0, so the pod still starts. |
| `mnemo-launcher exec -- <command>` | Asks the jar for the final command (`run --print --format nul`) and **replaces itself** with it, so the JVM is PID 1 and gets SIGTERM directly. On any doubt it starts your original command unchanged. |
| `mnemo-launcher jar <arguments>` | Runs any other CLI command, for example the trainer's `train`, as `java -jar mnemo-warmup.jar <arguments>` with no fallback. |

```yaml
initContainers:
  - name: mnemo-warmup-install
    image: ghcr.io/baokhang83/mnemo-warmup-tools:0.2.5
    command: ["/opt/mnemo-warmup/bin/mnemo-launcher", "install", "/mnemo-tools"]
    volumeMounts: [{ name: mnemo-tools, mountPath: /mnemo-tools }]
  - name: mnemo-warmup-fetch
    image: my-distroless-app:1.0
    command: ["/mnemo-tools/bin/mnemo-launcher", "fetch", "--jar", "/app/app.jar",
              "--store", "oci://registry.example.com/team/warmup", "--out", "/mnemo-cache"]
    volumeMounts: [{ name: mnemo-tools, mountPath: /mnemo-tools }, { name: mnemo-cache, mountPath: /mnemo-cache }]
containers:
  - name: app
    image: my-distroless-app:1.0
    command: ["/mnemo-tools/bin/mnemo-launcher"]
    args: ["exec", "--", "java", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]
    env: [{ name: MNEMO_WARMUP_CACHE_DIR, value: /mnemo-cache }]
```

The launcher looks for `java` the way your command would: an explicit path in the command, then `PATH`,
then `JAVA_HOME`, then common JDK locations. It never substitutes a different JDK for an explicit path.

Known differences and limits:

- **`fetch --strict`** keeps a real failure status, including when `java` is missing or older than 21
  (127, or the jar's status). The shell launcher exits 0 there. Without `--strict` both exit 0.
- **No Java version check.** On Java older than 21 the jar fails to start, which takes the same fallback
  (`fetch` exits 0, `exec` starts your command), at the price of one wasted JVM start.
- **`install` has no fallback.** If it cannot write the volume it exits 1 and the pod waits, because the
  later containers have nothing to run. Without `java` in the application image `exec` cannot start the
  application either and exits 127.
- **The trainer needs Java 21+** in the application image; `jar train` fails visibly without it.
- **The helper JVM** that decides the final command is stopped after 60 seconds and your command is
  started unchanged.
- Cache files are mode 0600 and owned by the user that ran `fetch`, so run the application as that user.

`scripts/verify-image.sh` checks all of this on `gcr.io/distroless/java21-debian12`: install, train,
push, fetch, cache hit, cache miss, corrupt archives, an unsupported command, UTF-8 arguments, exit status and SIGTERM
(`docker stop` ends with exit 143 when the JVM received it).

## Kubernetes: the Helm chart and the trainer

[`deploy/helm/mnemo-warmup`](../deploy/helm/mnemo-warmup) renders the **trainer**: a CronJob that runs your
application image, plus the ServiceAccount, Role and RoleBinding it needs. It is deliberately a CronJob and not a Helm
hook, so a failing trainer can never fail or roll back a release. Each run executes
`mnemo-warmup train`: compute the fingerprint, stop if the store already has it, otherwise take a Kubernetes
`Lease` named after the fingerprint (so two trainers never train the same archive; an expired lease from a crashed
trainer is taken over), train, upload, release. A tag whose entry is incomplete (for example a missing blob) is
replaced rather than treated as done. It exits 0 for every outcome and logs which one happened.

The chart does **not** render your Deployment. Your own chart includes its named templates to add the init
containers, volumes, environment and the exec-wrapper entrypoint to your pod template (the chart's README has the
snippet, and [`deploy/helm/tests/parent`](../deploy/helm/tests/parent) is a working example):

```yaml
dependencies:
  - { name: mnemo-warmup, version: 0.2.5, repository: "https://baokhang83.github.io/mnemo-warmup/", alias: warmup }
```

The values that must match your Deployment are `app.image`, `app.jar`, `app.jvmArgs` and `app.env`: an archive is only
valid for that exact launch, and a mismatch is safe (the pod starts without the cache). The trainer's ServiceAccount
may only `get`, `create`, `update` and `delete` Leases in its own namespace; application pods need no extra RBAC.

`mnemo-warmup train` can also be run directly (`--lock none` outside a cluster). It needs the extracted layout and exits
0 for every outcome unless `--strict`.

Check the chart with `scripts/test-chart.sh` (needs `helm`; set `KUBE_CONTEXT` to also have a cluster's API server
validate every manifest). See [ADR 0005](adr/0005-trainer-and-chart.md).

## Example and end-to-end test

[`examples/`](../examples/README.md) has a small Spring Boot application, an example workload chart that uses the
mnemo-warmup chart, and `scripts/e2e-kind.sh`, which runs the whole chain on a kind cluster for JDK 21 (AppCDS) and
JDK 25 (AOT): the app starts without an archive; the trainer trains and uploads once and releases its Lease; a second run
finds the entry complete; after a restart `fetch` finds the archive, the application's own classes load from it and `java`
is PID 1; and a JVM option changed only in the Deployment makes the pod start uncached, healthy, with a logged reason.

## The manifest and fingerprint

`build` writes `mnemo-warmup.manifest.json` next to the archive. It records what the archive
was trained against, and a `fingerprint` (`sha256:...`) derived from it:

- the cache type and the JDK vendor and full build,
- the optional `--image-digest`,
- the JVM options that can invalidate an archive: heap size and percentages, GC choice,
  `ObjectAlignmentInBytes`, compressed oops/class pointers, compact object headers. This is a
  deliberately conservative list (it also reads `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` and `JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS`);
  [#20](https://github.com/baokhang83/mnemo-warmup/issues/20) will measure which of these really
  matter, and others such as `-D` properties are ignored,
- every classpath entry in order, with its size and SHA-256 (the launched JAR plus what its
  `Class-Path` lists, which is the `lib/` directory for an extracted Spring Boot JAR).

File modification times, the directory the app was launched from, and the JDK's install path are
recorded but are not part of the fingerprint, because they can legitimately differ between a trainer
and a replica. `run` checks the modification times and the launch directory separately, since the
JVM does. Editing the file by hand makes it fail to load, because the recorded fingerprint no
longer matches. The manifest also stores the archive's size and SHA-256.

## What works today

- Target-JDK detection (`--java-home`, `$JAVA_HOME`, or the running JVM) and the choice
  between AppCDS and the AOT cache.
- Spring Boot fat-JAR extraction on the target JDK.
- The training runner: starts the app with the recording flag, waits for the exit mode,
  stops it with SIGTERM so the JVM writes the archive, and verifies the archive exists.
- Exit modes `spring-refresh` and `http-probe`.
- The manifest and fingerprint, and a function that explains how two environments differ.
- `bench`, `push` and `fetch` against an OCI registry (checked against a real `registry:2`), and `run`
  with the exec wrapper (a real JVM was started with a planned archive and loaded classes from it).
- `warmup-core` is on [Maven Central](https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/io.github.baokhang83.mnemo/warmup-core)
  as `io.github.baokhang83.mnemo:warmup-core`.

Not there yet: a published Helm chart (use `deploy/helm/mnemo-warmup` from this repository), results on amd64, and
more than one application (see the [project plan](PLAN.md)).

## Limitations

- **Tested on amd64 and arm64:** CI runs on Linux amd64 (the whole chain on a kind cluster, JDK 21 and 25); local runs were on arm64
  (Apple silicon, Docker, kind).
- **Linux and macOS only.** Stopping the app with SIGTERM is what makes the JVM write the
  archive; Windows kills the process instead.
- **AOT needs JDK 25+.** JDK 24 has the AOT cache but a two-step flow that is not
  supported yet; it uses AppCDS.
- **Spring Boot is tested with one small application** (the example, a web app with one controller), on JDK 21 and 25.
  To check your own Spring Boot 3.3+ JAR, run
  `mvn verify -pl warmup-core -Dwarmup.test.springBootJar=/path/to/app.jar`.
- AppCDS behaviour on JDK 21-24 was checked in Docker ([results](appcds-jdk-matrix.md)); CI runs
  the tests on 21 and 25.
- **Registry login:** Docker-config Basic/Bearer auth, and Amazon ECR through EKS IRSA ([setup](aws-workload-identity.md)).
  EKS Pod Identity, GKE, AKS and credential helpers are not implemented. The ECR path is tested against local
  fakes and AWS's SigV4 test vectors, not yet against a live EKS/ECR; other registries were tested without TLS.
- **Archives are never deleted.** Storage grows by one archive per fingerprint; see [archive retention](archive-retention.md) for bounding it with a registry lifecycle policy.
- **`run` hashes the classpath JARs and the archive at start.** That costs startup time on a large
  classpath; it has not been measured yet.

## Getting it

- **The tool in a pod:** the tools image `ghcr.io/baokhang83/mnemo-warmup-tools:<version>` (see [Container image](#container-image)),
  published for each release tag. It is the only way the CLI is distributed; build from source to run it elsewhere.
- **As a library:** `warmup-core` is on Maven Central (`io.github.baokhang83.mnemo:warmup-core`), for example for
  mnemo-jvm-warden.
- **The Helm chart:** a Helm repository, `helm repo add mnemo-warmup https://baokhang83.github.io/mnemo-warmup/`; the chart version is the release version.

`mnemo-warmup --version` prints the version of the jar you run.

## Repository layout

```
warmup-core/   engine: JDK detection, extraction, training, manifest, OCI store, fetch/run logic
warmup-cli/    command-line interface (picocli): build, bench, push, fetch, run, train
coverage/      aggregates JaCoCo coverage for the badge (not published)
image/         Dockerfile and shell launcher of the tools image
launcher/      the static Go launcher (mnemo-launcher) for shell-free images
deploy/helm/   Helm chart for the trainer plus the reusable pod-template helpers, and a parent-chart test fixture
examples/      a Spring Boot app, an example workload chart, and the notes behind scripts/e2e-kind.sh
scripts/       mnemo-warmup-exec wrapper, verify-image.sh, test-chart.sh, Docker checks for the AppCDS matrix
docs/PLAN.md   design, decisions and roadmap
docs/adr/      decisions: archive store, training trigger, run/exec model
```
