<!-- docs/helm-chart.md -->

# Deploy with the Helm chart

This is the explicit setup: you add the mnemo-warmup chart as a dependency of your application's chart and wire its helpers into your Deployment. Use it when you want to see and own the generated YAML, or for images that have `/bin/sh` and a Helm chart you already control. For the quickest start, with no template changes and with shell-free (distroless) images, use the annotation path described in the [README](../README.md) and [configuration](configuration.md) instead.

The chart's version is the release version: chart `0.2.5` deploys the `0.2.5` tools image ([release notes](https://github.com/baokhang83/mnemo-warmup/releases/tag/v0.2.5)). This path is unchanged since 0.2.0.

**Requirements specific to the chart:** the application image needs `/bin/sh` (the chart's launcher and wrapper are shell scripts) and Java 21 or newer. Everything else is in [configuration](configuration.md#requirements).

## Set up the chart

The chart is published as a Helm repository.

### 1. Fix the JARs when you build the image

An archive remembers the JAR files it was trained on, so the trainer and every pod must run the same files. For Spring Boot, extract
the JAR at build time:

```dockerfile
RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar target/app.jar extract --destination /out
...
COPY --from=build /out /app
CMD ["java", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]
```

Build one image per JDK you run: the image's JDK decides the cache type (AppCDS on 21 and later, the AOT cache on 25).

### 2. Add the chart to your application's chart

```bash
helm repo add mnemo-warmup https://baokhang83.github.io/mnemo-warmup/
helm search repo mnemo-warmup              # mnemo-warmup/mnemo-warmup  0.2.5
```

```yaml
# your-chart/Chart.yaml
dependencies:
  - name: mnemo-warmup
    version: 0.2.5
    repository: https://baokhang83.github.io/mnemo-warmup/
    alias: warmup
```

### 3. Create the namespace and the Secrets

The Secrets must exist in the namespace you deploy to, before you deploy (a missing Secret keeps the pod from starting). Two of them let the tool
talk to the **archive** registry (skip them only for an anonymous registry): the pull Secret needs read access to the archive repository, the push
Secret read and write. They are mounted into containers and do **not** authenticate image pulls, which the kubelet does with `imagePullSecrets`.
If your application image is in a private registry, create an image-pull Secret as well (it may hold the same credentials):

```bash
export NS=my-namespace
kubectl create namespace $NS
kubectl -n $NS create secret docker-registry warmup-pull --docker-server=registry.example.com --docker-username=... --docker-password=...
kubectl -n $NS create secret docker-registry warmup-push --docker-server=registry.example.com --docker-username=... --docker-password=...
kubectl -n $NS create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=registry.example.com --docker-username=... --docker-password=...   # image pulls
```

### 4. Set the values

```yaml
# your-chart/values.yaml
warmup:
  app:
    image: { repository: registry.example.com/team/my-app, tag: "1.4.2" }  # the SAME image your Deployment runs
    imagePullSecrets: [{ name: regcred }]   # for that image if it is private; the trainer uses it, and so does the Deployment below
    jar: /app/app.jar
    jvmArgs: ["-Xmx512m"]          # the heap/GC options your app really runs with; the Deployment's java command is built from this list
  store:
    url: oci://registry.example.com/team/warmup     # where archives are kept
    pullSecret: warmup-pull                          # omit both for an anonymous registry
    pushSecret: warmup-push
  trainer:
    exitMode: spring-refresh       # use http-probe (and trainer.probe.url) for apps that are not Spring Boot
```

The trainer runs your application for real, so it needs your configuration too (`warmup.trainer.env`, `envFrom`, `volumes`, `volumeMounts`).
If your Deployment sets `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` or `JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS`, repeat them in `warmup.app.env`: they are part of what an archive is valid for.

### 5. Wire your Deployment

The helpers print list items, so put each `include` **inside the list you already have** and keep your own entries next to them. A complete example is
[`examples/helm/example-app`](../examples/helm/example-app/templates/deployment.yaml).

```yaml
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      {{- with .Values.warmup.app.imagePullSecrets }}
      imagePullSecrets:
        {{- toYaml . | nindent 8 }}
      {{- end }}
      volumes:
        # ...your own volumes...
        {{- include "mnemo-warmup.volumes" .Values.warmup | nindent 8 }}
      initContainers:
        # ...your own init containers, if any...
        {{- include "mnemo-warmup.installInitContainer" .Values.warmup | nindent 8 }}
        {{- include "mnemo-warmup.fetchInitContainer" .Values.warmup | nindent 8 }}
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: {{ include "mnemo-warmup.appImage" .Values.warmup | quote }}
          command: {{ include "mnemo-warmup.command" .Values.warmup }}     # the wrapper decides, then execs java
          args:                                                              # your original command, moved here
            - java
            {{- range .Values.warmup.app.jvmArgs }}
            - {{ . | quote }}
            {{- end }}
            - -jar
            - {{ .Values.warmup.app.jar | quote }}
          env:
            # ...your own env...
            {{- include "mnemo-warmup.env" .Values.warmup | nindent 12 }}
          volumeMounts:
            # ...your own mounts...
            {{- include "mnemo-warmup.volumeMounts" .Values.warmup | nindent 12 }}
```

The wrapper replaces the container's entrypoint, so whatever `command` and `args` the container had (or the image's `ENTRYPOINT`) must become the
`java ...` arguments above. Options that do not affect an archive (`-D` properties, logging) can be added after the `jvmArgs` loop.

#### Optional: no init containers (`tools.delivery: image-volume`)

Set `warmup.tools.delivery: image-volume` to mount the tools image as an image volume and fetch in the application container's own entrypoint
([ADR 0012](adr/0012-tools-as-an-image-volume.md)). The two init container templates then render nothing, `volumes`, `volumeMounts` and `command` change
by themselves, and **one line is added to `args`**, before your own command:

```yaml
          args:
            {{- include "mnemo-warmup.argsPrefix" .Values.warmup | nindent 12 }}   # renders nothing in the default mode
            - java
            ...
```

That line is harmless in the default mode, so a Deployment written with it works in both. The mode needs a cluster and runtime with image volume support
(Kubernetes 1.33+, containerd 2.1+ or CRI-O 1.31+); a pod on a cluster without it does not start. It cannot be used with `store.pullSecret`, because the
application container would then be able to read the Secret: the chart refuses to render the combination. See the
[annotation reference](configuration.md#tools-delivery-init-containers-or-an-image-volume) for the full list of what changes.

### 6. Deploy, train, then check

```bash
helm dependency update your-chart
helm upgrade --install my-app your-chart -n $NS
kubectl -n $NS get cronjob                                         # the trainer, e.g. my-app-warmup-trainer
kubectl -n $NS create job first-train --from=cronjob/my-app-warmup-trainer
kubectl -n $NS wait --for=condition=complete job/first-train --timeout=15m
kubectl -n $NS logs job/first-train -c trainer                     # must say: train: TRAINED ...  (FAILED prints the reason)
```

The trainer also runs every 10 minutes by itself (`warmup.trainer.schedule`). Pods that start before the first archive exists run without it.
Only when the outcome says `TRAINED` (or `ALREADY_STORED`), restart the pods and look at what they did:

```bash
kubectl -n $NS rollout restart deploy/my-app
kubectl -n $NS logs <new-pod> -c mnemo-warmup-fetch     # Archive: ... (APP_CDS)    or    (LEYDEN_AOT) on JDK 25
                                                         # (with tools.delivery=image-volume there is no such container: grep the app log for "Archive:")
kubectl -n $NS logs <new-pod> -c app | grep "run:"      # run: using APP_CDS archive ...
```

## Disable or remove it

Suspending the trainer (`warmup.trainer.suspend: true`) only stops **new training**: pods keep fetching and using the archives that already exist. To stop
using the cache:

1. Take the `include` lines out of your Deployment (including `argsPrefix`, if you added it) and restore its original `command` and `args`; redeploy. New pods
   start without the init containers, the wrapper or the cache.
2. Set `warmup.trainer.enabled: false` (or remove the dependency) to delete the trainer CronJob, its ServiceAccount and its Role.
3. Optionally delete the archives from the registry (tags `fp-<hex>` in the archive repository) and any Leases left behind
   (`kubectl -n $NS get lease | grep mnemo-warmup`; they expire on their own).



---

<!-- docs/registry-auth.md -->

# Registry authentication

The tool talks to the **archive** registry from inside pods: the `fetch` init container needs **pull** access, the trainer **pull and push** access. These credentials are separate from the ones your cluster uses to pull container images; image-pull credentials are used by the kubelet and are not visible to the containers.

Use separate pull and push credentials. A read-only credential should not be able to overwrite archives.

## How a login is chosen

For a registry, in this order:

1. **A Docker-config entry for the registry host**, from the mounted Secret (`--registry-auth`, or `$MNEMO_WARMUP_REGISTRY_AUTH`). It is used as is.
2. Otherwise, for an **Amazon ECR** host in a pod that has an EKS web identity, a login obtained from that identity ([below](#eks-and-ecr)).
3. Otherwise the access is anonymous.

If a login is missing or refused, `fetch` logs the reason and the pod starts without a cache; the trainer logs it and exits 0.

## Docker-config Secrets

Create `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` Secrets in the workload's namespace **before** you deploy. A pod that mounts a Secret that does not exist cannot start.

```bash
kubectl -n my-namespace create secret docker-registry warmup-pull \
  --docker-server=registry.example.com --docker-username=... --docker-password=...
kubectl -n my-namespace create secret docker-registry warmup-push \
  --docker-server=registry.example.com --docker-username=... --docker-password=...
```

Reference them from the Deployment's pod template:

```yaml
warmup.mnemo.io/pull-secret: "warmup-pull"
warmup.mnemo.io/push-secret: "warmup-push"
```

Basic and Bearer-token registries are supported. Credential helpers are not.

## EKS and ECR

On EKS, give the application's service account a **pull** role and the trainer's service account a **push** role through IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA). The tool exchanges the pod's web identity for an ECR login, caches it until shortly before it expires and refreshes it, including mid-run. No password is stored anywhere. The full setup, with the trust and permission policies and a verification checklist, is in the [EKS and ECR guide](aws-workload-identity.md).

For the annotation path, the trainer's CronJob uses its own generated ServiceAccount. Annotate it with the push role after the first render (for example with a Helm post-renderer or a Kustomize patch), because the injector does not set service account annotations. The application's own service account carries the pull role.

Verified so far: the ECR path against local fakes and AWS's SigV4 test vectors. **Not yet verified on a live EKS and ECR.**

## Other registries

Docker-config Secrets work with registries that accept Basic or Bearer-token login. GKE, AKS and EKS Pod Identity are not implemented; the provider boundary they would plug into is described in [ADR 0008](adr/0008-registry-auth-providers.md).


---

<!-- docs/aws-workload-identity.md -->

# Amazon ECR with EKS workload identity

mnemo-warmup can log in to an Amazon ECR archive store with the identity of the pod, so no registry password is stored in a Secret. It uses IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA) on EKS. GKE and AKS are not supported yet, and EKS Pod Identity is not supported yet.

This guide has not been verified against a live EKS cluster and ECR registry in this repository's CI. The unit tests use local fakes for STS, ECR and the registry, and the signing code is checked against AWS's published SigV4 test vectors. Run the checklist at the end on your cluster before relying on it.

## How it works

1. EKS injects `AWS_ROLE_ARN` and `AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE` into a pod whose service account is annotated with an IAM role.
2. When the registry host is an ECR host (`<account>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com`, also `ecr-fips` and the `.cn` suffix), mnemo-warmup reads the token file and calls STS `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` in the same region. The region comes from the registry host.
3. It signs an ECR `GetAuthorizationToken` call with the temporary keys, caches the resulting login for its roughly 12-hour lifetime, and refreshes it five minutes before expiry. A registry that rejects a login mid-run triggers one refresh.
4. No credential is ever written to a log or error message.

A `--registry-auth` file (or `$MNEMO_WARMUP_REGISTRY_AUTH`) with an entry for the registry still takes precedence. With neither a file entry nor a web identity, access is anonymous as before.

## Set up two roles

Use a pull-only role for the application's `fetch` and a push role for the trainer, so a compromised application cannot overwrite archives.

Trust policy for each role (replace the placeholders):

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": { "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::<account>:oidc-provider/<oidc-issuer-host-and-path>" },
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
    "Condition": { "StringEquals": {
      "<oidc-issuer-host-and-path>:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com",
      "<oidc-issuer-host-and-path>:sub": "system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service-account>"
    } }
  }]
}
```

Permissions for the **pull** role:

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "ecr:GetAuthorizationToken", "Resource": "*" },
    { "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability", "ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer", "ecr:BatchGetImage"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:ecr:<region>:<account>:repository/<archive-repository>" }
  ]
}
```

The **push** role adds `ecr:InitiateLayerUpload`, `ecr:UploadLayerPart`, `ecr:CompleteLayerUpload` and `ecr:PutImage` on the same repository. ECR does not create repositories on push: create `<archive-repository>` first.

## Attach the roles

- **Trainer (Helm chart):** annotate the trainer's service account with the push role.

  ```yaml
  trainer:
    serviceAccount:
      annotations:
        eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::<account>:role/mnemo-warmup-push
  ```

- **Application (fetch):** the `fetch` init container runs in the application's pod, so it uses the application's service account. Annotate that service account with the pull role. Leave the store's `pullSecret` and `pushSecret` empty.

## Optional second role

To start from one identity and act as another (a role in a different account, for example), set `MNEMO_WARMUP_AWS_ROLE_ARN` on the container. mnemo-warmup then calls STS `AssumeRole` with the web identity's keys before asking ECR for a login. The pod's role needs `sts:AssumeRole` on the target role, and the target's trust policy must name the pod's role.

## Other settings

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| `AWS_ROLE_SESSION_NAME` | STS session name (default `mnemo-warmup`). |
| `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_STS`, `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_ECR` | Override the endpoints, for VPC endpoints or tests. Defaults are the regional `sts.<region>` and `api.ecr.<region>` hosts, with `.com.cn` in China. |

## What happens on failure

`fetch` treats every login problem (missing token file, denied permission, STS or ECR down) as "no archive": it prints the reason to stderr and the application starts without a cache, exit code 0 (`--strict` exits 1). Transient errors (connection failures, HTTP 429 and 5xx) get up to three attempts; permission errors are not retried.

## Verify on your cluster

1. `kubectl exec` into a pod using the annotated service account and confirm `AWS_ROLE_ARN` and `AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE` are set.
2. Run the trainer once and check the archive appears in ECR under the tag `fp-<hex>`.
3. Start the application and check the `fetch` log for `Archive:` rather than a `fetch:` note.
4. Remove `ecr:PutImage` from the push role and confirm the trainer reports the denial and the application still starts.

Not yet confirmed outside local fakes: the STS JSON response format (we send `Accept: application/json`) and ECR's registry behaviour on token expiry.


---

<!-- docs/archive-retention.md -->

# Keeping archive storage bounded

mnemo-warmup stores one archive per fingerprint in an OCI registry and never deletes anything. This guide explains how the store grows, what deleting an archive costs, and how to bound growth with your registry's own lifecycle policy. mnemo-warmup adds no delete command and needs no delete permission for any of this: the registry applies the policy itself, with its own authority.

## How the store grows

- Each fingerprint is one tag, `fp-<64 hex characters>`, on a manifest with two blobs: a small config blob (the manifest JSON) and the archive itself, typically hundreds of MB ([ADR 0001](adr/0001-archive-store.md)).
- The fingerprint covers the JDK build, the classpath, the JVM flags, the cache type and the image digest when one is given. A new image build, a JDK patch release or a changed JVM flag therefore produces a new fingerprint and a new archive. Old fingerprints are never reused or overwritten by newer ones.
- Growth is roughly *archives per release x number of releases x archive size*. For illustration: 300 MB per archive, one archive per release (AppCDS), 20 releases a month is about 6 GB a month. Measure your own archive size with `mnemo-warmup build` before deciding on a budget.

## What deleting an archive costs

Deleting an archive costs a cache miss, not an outage ([constitution](fluencyloop/constitution.md) §1 and §3):

1. A pod whose fingerprint is gone gets "no archive" from `fetch` and starts the application with an ordinary JVM start, as if it had never been trained.
2. The trainer finds the tag missing on its next scheduled run, trains again and pushes the archive back, so later pods are cached again.

So the cost of a wrong deletion is slower starts for every pod that starts between the deletion and the next successful training run, plus one training run. It is worth avoiding for a version that is running or that you may roll back to, but nothing fails.

## What to keep in mind before you delete

- **Scope the policy to the archive repository.** Use a repository that holds only mnemo-warmup archives, and match only `fp-` tags. Never apply a rule to a repository that also holds application images.
- **Do not add a rule for untagged images.** The trainer uploads blobs before it creates the tag. Leave removal of unreferenced blobs to the registry's own garbage collection, which is not something this guide has verified for any registry.
- **Tags are mutable by design.** The tag name is derived from the content's fingerprint, so a tag normally always points at the same archive. The trainer pushes a tag again only to repair an incomplete entry. With a registry setting that makes tags immutable, that repair push is not covered by any test here.
- **Shared consumers.** Fingerprints do not record which application or environment created them. If several applications, clusters or environments share one repository, a busy application's frequent builds can push other applications' archives out of a "newest N" window. Use one repository per application or team, or size N for the busiest consumer.
- **Active deployments and rollbacks.** A lifecycle rule cannot see which fingerprints are running or are rollback targets. A rule that keeps the newest N archives by push time only protects the most recent builds. A release that has been running for months can fall outside the window, and so can the version you roll back to after a series of bad releases.
- **Age-based expiry does not protect active versions.** An expiry-after-N-days rule (a TTL) deletes archives by how long ago they were pushed. It does not know whether the version is still deployed, so a stable release that was not rebuilt for N days loses its archive while it keeps running. Do not read a TTL as "unused for N days". Use a count-based rule, or set the TTL far longer than your oldest running release.
- **Ongoing uploads.** The newest archive is never among the oldest N, so a count-based rule does not select an upload that has just completed. Registries evaluate lifecycle rules on their own schedule, so do not rely on an exact moment.
- **Choose N from your deployments.** N should be at least the number of fingerprints that can be live at once (versions and cache types in flight across all environments sharing the repository) plus the rollback depth you want. The example below uses 30 as a placeholder, not a recommendation for your workload.

## Example: Amazon ECR

[`examples/ecr-lifecycle-policy.json`](examples/ecr-lifecycle-policy.json) keeps the newest 30 images in the repository whose tag matches `fp-*` and expires older ones:

```json
{
  "rules": [
    {
      "rulePriority": 1,
      "description": "Keep the newest 30 mnemo-warmup archives (tags fp-*); expire older ones",
      "selection": {
        "tagStatus": "tagged",
        "tagPatternList": ["fp-*"],
        "countType": "imageCountMoreThan",
        "countNumber": 30
      },
      "action": { "type": "expire" }
    }
  ]
}
```

What the AWS documentation confirms about this policy:

- The structure above (`rulePriority`, `selection`, `action`) and its fields. `tagPatternList` is the documented way to select tagged images, and `countUnit` must be omitted for `imageCountMoreThan`.
- `imageCountMoreThan` sorts images from youngest to oldest by push time and expires the ones beyond the count, always older before newer.
- Expiry happens within 24 hours after the criteria are met.
- A lifecycle policy applies to one repository in one Region.
- Actions are recorded in CloudTrail.

Apply it only after you have looked at what it would do:

1. Open the repository in the ECR console, choose lifecycle policy, paste the JSON and use **Save and run test**. The test lists the images the policy would expire without deleting anything.
2. Check that the listed archives are ones you can afford to lose, and that nothing outside `fp-` tags appears.
3. Apply it, either from the console or with `aws ecr put-lifecycle-policy --repository-name <name> --lifecycle-policy-text file://ecr-lifecycle-policy.json`.

Limitations that the AWS documentation does not settle, and that have not been tested with mnemo-warmup archives:

- Whether lifecycle rules treat these OCI artifacts (custom `artifactType` and config media type) the same as container images. The documentation speaks of "images" throughout.
- Whether pushing a tag again changes the push time used for ordering.
- Behaviour with immutable tags.
- That `sinceImagePulled` rules would count a `fetch` as a pull. Do not use a pull-based rule to protect active archives until you have checked it on your registry.
- The maximum number of rules and the policy size limit.

The Region matters: the policy only acts on the repository in the Region where you created it.

## Other registries

Most registries have a similar feature (Harbor retention rules, Google Artifact Registry cleanup policies, Azure Container Registry retention). Apply the same rules: a dedicated repository, match only `fp-` tags, count-based and conservative, preview before enabling, and check how the feature treats OCI artifacts and tag updates. This guide does not provide or verify policies for them.

## What this release does not do

- No automatic deletion and no `prune` command.
- No delete permission is granted to the fetch or trainer roles. The [ECR roles](aws-workload-identity.md) deliberately omit `ecr:BatchDeleteImage`.
- No tracking of which fingerprints are active, so retention cannot protect them for you.


---

<!-- docs/appcds-jdk-matrix.md -->

# AppCDS (dynamic archive) on JDK 21-24

Verified for issue #10 with `scripts/verify-appcds.sh` (Docker, `eclipse-temurin:<n>-jdk`, linux/arm64).
Builds tested: 21.0.13+9, 22.0.2+9, 23.0.2+7, 24.0.2+12. The app is a two-class JAR run by absolute
path. Training uses `-XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit`, runs use `-XX:SharedArchiveFile`.

## Result

**The same flags work on JDK 21, 22, 23 and 24.** `CacheStrategy` needs no per-JDK change.
Behaviour is identical on all four releases in every scenario below, except for the number of
classes loaded from the archive (13 on 22, 17 on the others), which only reflects the JDK's own
class set.

## What the JVM does when the archive does not match

"Archive used" means classes were loaded from `shared objects file (top)` (the dynamic layer).

| Scenario | `-Xshare:auto` (JVM default) | `-Xshare:on` |
|---|---|---|
| Same JAR, same flags | archive used | archive used |
| JAR modification time changed | **ignored**, exit 0, `[warning][cds]` line | exit 1 |
| Same bytes, new mtime (plain `cp`) | **ignored**, exit 0, warning | exit 1 |
| JAR content changed | **ignored**, exit 0, warning | exit 1 |
| JAR moved to another directory | archive used | archive used |
| Archive from another JDK build | **ignored**, exit 0, warning | exit 1 |
| Archive truncated | **ignored**, exit 0, warning | exit 1 |
| Archive file missing | ignored, exit 0, no message | exit 1 |
| `-Xmx40g` (no compressed oops) | **ignored, exit 0, no message** | exit 1 |
| `-XX:-UseCompressedClassPointers` | **ignored, exit 0, no message** | exit 1 |
| `-Xmx64m` | archive used | archive used |
| `-XX:+UseSerialGC` / `-XX:+UseParallelGC` (trained with default) | archive used | archive used |

## Consequences for the design

1. **The fallback promise in `PLAN.md` holds.** With the default `-Xshare:auto` a bad archive is
   never fatal. `-Xshare:on` is fatal in every case, so we must never pass it.
2. **Invalidation is all or nothing.** One changed JAR drops the whole archive. There is no partial use.
3. **JAR modification time matters, content equality does not.** A byte-identical JAR with a new
   mtime is rejected. This confirms the open question about mtimes (`PLAN.md`, question 6): trainer
   and runtime must use the same extracted files, or the same preserved mtimes.
4. **The JAR path is not checked** when the file is at the same relative layout, so moving the
   directory is safe (tested with an absolute path on both sides).
5. **Some mismatches are silent.** Heap size beyond the compressed-oops limit and
   compressed-class-pointer changes make the JVM drop the archive without a log line. A pod cannot
   tell "archive used" from "archive ignored" by exit code. Verification needs
   `-Xlog:class+load` or `-Xshare:auto -Xlog:cds`.
6. **Evidence for issue #20 (which flags to fingerprint).** For a dynamic archive, GC choice and a
   small `-Xmx` did not invalidate it here. Compressed oops and compressed class pointers did.
   `JvmFlags` keeps its conservative set until #20 measures this with a real Spring Boot app.

## Reproduce

```
scripts/verify-appcds.sh 21 22 23 24
```

Output is one tab-separated row per scenario and mode.

<!-- benchmarks/README.md -->

# Benchmarks

Measurements of what mnemo-warmup does to **pod start-to-Ready**, with the method, the raw data and the machine specification, so that anyone can rerun the study or check a number.

The question is not "does the JVM start faster with an archive" (it does). It is "does a *pod* become Ready sooner once you add the init containers, the archive download, the digest checks and the helper JVMs that the cache needs", and where the time goes.

## Method

`scripts/bench-cluster.sh` creates a throw-away [kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/) cluster and an archive registry (`registry:2` on the kind network), builds the tools image from this checkout and the application image, and deploys **three arms** of the same chart (`examples/annotated-app`), all running the same application image:

| arm | what runs |
|---|---|
| `none` | the plain Deployment, no mnemo-warmup |
| `nocache` | mnemo-warmup on (init containers, launcher, helper JVMs), but the archive repository is empty: the cost of the machinery with no benefit |
| `cached` | mnemo-warmup on and an archive trained for this image: what a real pod does |

Each **measurement** scales one Deployment from 0 to 1 (a brand-new pod), waits for Ready, records the pod's own timestamps and the tools' timing lines, then scales back to 0. The arms are **interleaved** (round 1: none, nocache, cached; round 2: ...), so slow drift of the machine affects all arms equally. One warm-up round per arm is discarded. The default is 12 measured rounds.

**Cold means:** a new pod on a node that already holds the image. Image pull time is **not** measured, because the same image is pulled in every arm and the cache does not change it. A pod on a node that must pull the image first is slower by that pull, in every arm.

**Where the numbers come from**

- *Coarse phases* come from the pod object (`status.startTime`, init and app container `startedAt` and `finishedAt`, the `Initialized` and `Ready` conditions). The API stores **whole seconds**, so a single coarse number can be off by up to a second; medians over many rounds are what to read. The readiness probe runs every second, which adds up to one second of quantisation to `Ready` as well.
- *Fine phases* (milliseconds) come from the tools themselves with `MNEMO_WARMUP_TIMING=1`: `fetch` reports JDK detection, extracting and hashing the classpath, and the store lookup, download and digest check; `run` reports reading the manifest, the SHA-256 of the archive, the JDK probe and hashing the classpath; the launcher reports the wall time of each helper process, which includes starting that helper's JVM. The application's own start-up is Spring's `Started ... in N seconds`.
- Every restart records whether the JVM actually used the archive, so a run where an arm did not behave as intended is visible (the *Validity* table in each summary).

## What is in this directory

```
benchmarks/
  README.md                this file
  spring-heavy/            the benchmark application: Spring Boot with web, JPA/Hibernate, security,
                           validation, actuator and caching (69 JARs), built as an extracted image
  results/<timestamp>-<app>[-<conditions>]/
    summary.md             the tables
    results.csv            one row per measured restart, every phase and timing
    environment.json       machine, Docker, kind node, Kubernetes, tool versions, git commit, exact command
    registry.txt           registry latency and archive download speed as seen from the node
    raw/<arm>-<round>.json         the pod object of that restart (as Kubernetes returned it)
    raw/<arm>-<round>.fetch.log    the fetch init container's log (timing line included)
    raw/<arm>-<round>.app.log      the application container's log (launcher and run timing, Spring start line)
```

## Reproduce it

Needs docker, kind, kubectl, Helm 3, Java 21 and Maven (to build the CLI), python3 and network access.

```bash
scripts/bench-cluster.sh                                  # 12 rounds, no pod limits
scripts/bench-cluster.sh --app-cpu 1 --app-memory 1Gi     # requests = limits on the application container
scripts/bench-cluster.sh --app example                    # the small example app instead
scripts/bench-cluster.sh --restarts 30 --out /tmp/mine    # more rounds, other output directory
KEEP=1 scripts/bench-cluster.sh                           # keep the cluster for poking around
```

To re-derive the tables from a stored run, with no cluster: `python3 scripts/bench_summarize.py benchmarks/results/<run>`. To check a number, open `results.csv` or the `raw/` pod JSON: every figure in `summary.md` is computed from them.

## Cluster specification

Recorded by `scripts/bench_env.py` in `environment.json` for every run: host CPU model, logical CPUs and memory; the CPUs and memory Docker gives its VM; the kind node image and its Docker and cgroup limits (`nano_cpus`, `cpu_quota`, `cpuset_cpus`, `memory_bytes`, `cpu.max`; 0 or `max` means unlimited); Kubernetes and containerd versions, node capacity and allocatable; the CPU and memory limits of the application container (`none` by default); tool versions; the git commit, and whether the tree had uncommitted changes; and the exact command. The pod QoS class and resources are in each `raw/*.json`.

Things to know when comparing with another environment:

- **Registry latency is a best case.** The registry is a container one network hop from the node; `registry.txt` records the request time and the archive download speed from the node. A registry in another zone, or ECR, adds its own round trips and a slower download, which falls entirely on the `cached` arm. This study does not measure that; the numbers here are a lower bound on the cache's cost.
- **No pod limits by default.** The JVM then sees all the CPUs Docker has. With `--app-cpu 1` it sees one, as in many production clusters, and starts much more slowly; that changes the benefit and, because the helper JVMs run in the *application* container's limits only if you set them there, not the cost. The injector does not copy resource limits to the generated `fetch` init container, so `fetch` is unlimited in both modes.
- **kind on Docker Desktop is a virtual machine on a laptop.** Timings are noisy and not representative of a production node. The point is the *shape* (which phases exist and how large they are relative to each other) and the paired comparison, not the absolute seconds.

## Limits of the study

- Three applications: a Spring Boot application, Jenkins LTS and SonarQube. Other frameworks and sizes are not covered (planned for the 0.3.0 beta).
- One JDK (21, AppCDS). The Leyden AOT cache on JDK 25 is not measured here.
- A local registry; no network cost, no authentication round trips (ECR's token exchange adds some).
- Image pulls excluded by design (see above).
- Single node, one pod at a time: no contention between replicas starting together, which is the autoscaling case where the cache could matter more.
- Arms differ only by mnemo-warmup; the application image is identical.

## Results

Runs are committed with their full `summary.md` (the end-to-end breakdown), `results.csv`, `environment.json`, `registry.txt` and the raw pod objects and logs. Every run: 12 measured rounds per arm, Apple M5 laptop, kind on Docker Desktop. Medians; pod timestamps have 1 s resolution.

| Run | Application | Limits | Tools delivery |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`20261111-spring-heavy-no-limits-clean`](results/20261111-spring-heavy-no-limits-clean/summary.md) | spring-heavy, JDK 21 | none | init containers (Java helpers) |
| [`20261111-spring-heavy-1cpu-1gi`](results/20261111-spring-heavy-1cpu-1gi/summary.md) | spring-heavy, JDK 21 | 1 CPU, 1 GiB | init containers (Java helpers) |
| [`20261111-spring-heavy-1cpu-1gi-native`](results/20261111-spring-heavy-1cpu-1gi-native/summary.md) | spring-heavy, JDK 21 | 1 CPU, 1 GiB | init containers (native `fetch` and `run`) |
| [`20261111-spring-heavy-1cpu-1gi-imagevolume`](results/20261111-spring-heavy-1cpu-1gi-imagevolume/summary.md) | spring-heavy, JDK 21 | 1 CPU, 1 GiB | `image` volume |
| [`20261111-jenkins-1cpu-1gi`](results/20261111-jenkins-1cpu-1gi/summary.md) | Jenkins 2.492.3, JDK 21 | 1 CPU, 1 GiB | init containers (Java helpers); header says "0 JARs", a harness bug fixed since |
| [`20261111-jenkins-1cpu-1gi-native`](results/20261111-jenkins-1cpu-1gi-native/summary.md) | Jenkins 2.492.3, JDK 21 | 1 CPU, 1 GiB | init containers (native helpers) |
| [`20261111-jenkins-1cpu-1gi-imagevolume`](results/20261111-jenkins-1cpu-1gi-imagevolume/summary.md) | Jenkins 2.492.3, JDK 21 | 1 CPU, 1 GiB | `image` volume |
| [`20261111-sonarqube-2cpu-3gi`](results/20261111-sonarqube-2cpu-3gi/summary.md) | SonarQube 26.11, JDK 25 | 2 CPU, 3 GiB | init containers (native helpers) |

### The baseline, and what changed

The first two runs measured the original Java helpers. The archive shortened the application's own start by 0.6 to 1.3 s, but pod start-to-Ready did not improve, because the helpers cost about 1 s:

| spring-heavy | no limits | 1 CPU / 1 GiB |
|---|---|---|
| Pod start-to-Ready, `none` / `nocache` / `cached` | 3 s / 4 s / 4 s | 5 s / 6 s / 5 s |
| Application start (`Started ... in`), without / with the archive | 1318 ms / 696 ms | 3136 ms / 1872 ms |
| Time the helpers take before the app starts, `cached` | about 990 ms | about 1050 ms |

Native `fetch` and `run` (Go, [ADR 0010](../docs/adr/0010-native-run-planner.md) and [0011](../docs/adr/0011-native-fetch.md)) brought the helpers from about 1050 ms to about 140 ms. What remains is Kubernetes sequencing the init containers (about 1.75 s from the pod to the application container starting, of which our code is about 0.1 s). Delivering the tools as an `image` volume removes the init containers ([ADR 0012](../docs/adr/0012-tools-as-an-image-volume.md)).

### Three applications at 1 CPU / 1 GiB (SonarQube at 2 CPU / 3 GiB)

Pod start-to-Ready, medians (range), by delivery mode:

| Application | `none` | init containers: `nocache` / `cached` | `image` volume: `nocache` / `cached` | Application start without / with the archive |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| spring-heavy | 4.5 s (init run), 5 s (`image` volume run) | 6 s / 5 s | 5 s / **3 s (3-4)** | 3186 ms / 1888 ms |
| Jenkins | 4 s (3-5) | 5 s / 5 s | 5 s / 4 s (3-5) | 2334 ms / 2025 ms |
| SonarQube | 15 s (14-16) | 16 s / 17 s | not run | not meaningful (see below) |

`none` differed by up to 0.5 s between runs of the same application, which is the noise floor at this timestamp resolution.

- **spring-heavy.** With the `image` volume the pod with a trained archive is ready 2 s (40%) sooner than the pod without mnemo-warmup. With init containers it is not.
- **Jenkins.** The archive saves about 0.3 s of a 2.3 s start (85% of its classes already load from the archive; the rest of the start is initialization). Pod readiness is at parity with the `image` volume and 1 s slower with init containers.
- **SonarQube.** The archive was used in 12 of 12 pods and `cached` minus `nocache` was 0 s: it covers only the small coordinator JVM, and the three JVMs that do the work are started by it ([issue #77](https://github.com/baokhang83/mnemo-warmup/issues/77)). With init containers `cached` is 1 s (range 1 to 3) slower than no mnemo-warmup. One earlier training run did not report `TRAINED` and the cause was not found; the harness now keeps `raw/train.log`.

**What this does not say.** Laptop, local registry, no image pull, one pod at a time. It says nothing about a remote registry (which would make `cached` slower), or about many pods starting together. The 0.3.0 beta plans a scale-out burst against a remote registry, an application-size study and a JDK 21 against JDK 25 comparison.

Two earlier runs were discarded because other benchmark runs were active on the same machine; all published runs ran alone.


---

<!-- docs/PLAN.md -->

# mnemo-warmup: project plan (v3, Kubernetes init container, AppCDS and/or AOT)

Cluster-aware startup caches for JVM workloads on Kubernetes: AppCDS (`.jsa`) and
Project Leyden AOT cache (`.aot`), trained once and shared by every replica through an
init container, with a safe fallback to a normal start.
Part of the Mnemo suite (`mnemo-jvm-warden`, `mnemo-cache`, `mnemo-warmup`).

> History: v2 dropped the Maven plugin for a Kubernetes-first design. v3 makes the
> cache type explicit: AppCDS and AOT are both first-class, selected per workload.

## Problem
AppCDS / Leyden AOT caches cut JVM startup 30-60%, but are rarely used:
- Producing an archive needs a training run (unpack, start, drive code paths, clean exit).
- Archives are bound to the exact JDK build, classpath and JVM flags; a mismatch
  silently disables them or fails startup.
- Training in CI lacks real config, secrets and dependencies.
- Nobody measures the savings.

## Core idea
Train once per fingerprint in the real cluster, store the archive, and have every
replica fetch it in an init container before the app starts. If no valid archive
exists, the pod boots normally. Never crash because of a cache.

Fingerprint = `(image digest, JDK vendor and build, cache type, classpath hashes, GC and heap flags)`.

## Cache types

AppCDS and the Leyden AOT cache are alternatives, not layers: the JVM is given one
archive per run (`-XX:SharedArchiveFile` or `-XX:AOTCache`). The AOT cache builds on the
CDS machinery and stores more (linked classes, and on JDK 25+ method profiles).

| JDK | AppCDS (`.jsa`) | AOT cache (`.aot`) |
|---|---|---|
| 21-23 | Supported (dynamic archive) | Not available |
| 24 | Supported | Exists, but needs two-step record/create; **not supported in v1** |
| 25+ | Supported (fallback) | **Preferred**, single step via `-XX:AOTCacheOutput` (JEP 514) |

- `cacheType: auto` (default): AOT on JDK 25+, AppCDS otherwise.
- `cacheType: appcds` or `aot`: force one. Forcing `aot` on JDK < 25 is a config error
  reported by the trainer and init container, and the app still starts uncached.
- Both can be trained for the same image (separate fingerprints). This lets `bench`
  compare them, and lets a rollout fall back from AOT to AppCDS if the AOT archive is
  rejected.
- The type is part of the fingerprint and the manifest.

Fallback chain at pod start: matching AOT archive, then matching AppCDS archive, then
plain JVM start. The JVM's own default behaviour on a mismatched archive is to ignore it
and continue; we never set flags that make a bad archive fatal.

## Architecture

```
            +-----------------------+
 trainer    | trainer Job           |  runs app with training flags, clean exit
 (once per  | (mnemo-warmup build)  |--------------------+
 fingerprint)+----------------------+                    v
                                             +------------------------+
                                             | archive store          |
                                             | key = fingerprint      |
                                             | (OCI / S3 / PVC)       |
                                             +------------------------+
                                                         |
 every pod:  init container (mnemo-warmup fetch) <-------+  lookup, verify manifest
                |
                v  writes archive + env file to shared emptyDir
          app container: java <archive flag> ...   (or plain start if nothing matched)
```

How the app picks up the archive: the init container writes the archive and a small
flags file into the `emptyDir`. The app container either runs through
`mnemo-warmup run` (preferred; validates the manifest against live JDK and flags, then
execs `java`) or sets `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` from the flags file (no entrypoint change, less
validation).

Components:
- **core** (Java 21+): JDK detection, cache type selection, fat-JAR extraction, training
  runner, fingerprint and manifest, bench.
- **cli**: `build`, `bench`, `fetch`, `run`.
- **image**: JDK-free tools image carrying the CLI, the shell launcher and exec wrapper, and the static native
  launcher (`launcher/`) for shell-free images into the application image (`docs/adr/0004-tools-image.md`); the tool runs inside the app image.
- **deploy/helm**: chart adding the init container, volume and trainer Job.
- **Injection into workloads:** lives in `mnemo-jvm-warden` (see below), not in this repo.

## Relationship to mnemo-jvm-warden

`mnemo-jvm-warden` (Java) already ships a controller, CRDs (`WardenPolicy`,
`WardenBoost`), a sidecar and Helm charts, and publishes to Maven Central. Warden shrinks
and grows running pods in place without restarts; warmup speeds up the pods that do start
(deploys, scale-ups, node moves). They are complementary but separate:

- Separate repos. Warmup is usable without warden (plain init-container snippet).
- Integration is by library: warden depends on `warmup-core` (fingerprint and manifest
  API) in-process, instead of shelling out to the CLI.
- Injecting the init container into workloads is a warden feature (for example a
  `WardenPolicy` field), so no second controller or webhook is built here.
- Open technical question: which JVM flags change an archive's validity. If
  `SoftMaxHeapSize` does not, one archive can survive warden's day/night resizes.

## Open decisions
1. **Archive store:** DECIDED: OCI registry first, behind a put/get/exists interface
   (see `docs/adr/0001-archive-store.md`). S3/GCS may follow; RWX PVC not planned.
2. **Who trains:** DECIDED: chart-owned CronJob with a Lease, non-hook (see
   `docs/adr/0002-training-trigger-and-traffic.md`).
3. **Training traffic:** DECIDED: `spring-refresh` default, `http-probe` opt-in, no warmup
   script in v0.2.0 (same ADR).
4. **App pickup:** DECIDED: `run` is supported; `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` from the flags file works
   but is unvalidated (see `docs/adr/0003-run-exec-model-and-layout.md`).
5. **AppCDS flavour:** dynamic archive on top of the JDK default archive vs static
   dump. Dynamic is simpler. Verified on 21-24: see `docs/appcds-jdk-matrix.md`.
6. **JAR modification times:** DECIDED: extract at image build time so trainer and runtime share
   the same files; `run` compares modification times and starts plain on a difference (same ADR).

## Repo layout
```
warmup-core/  warmup-cli/  image/  deploy/helm/  examples/  docs/
```
Maven coordinates: groupId `io.github.baokhang83.mnemo` (same as warden), artifacts
`warmup-core` and `warmup-cli`.

## Roadmap

### Phase 1: engine and CLI (v0.1.0)
- [x] Maven reactor scaffold, JDK detection and flag selection (`CacheStrategy`)
- [x] `cacheType` option (`auto`, `appcds`, `aot`) with validation against the JDK
- [x] Spring Boot fat-JAR extraction (`-Djarmode=tools extract`)
- [x] Training runner for both types, exit modes: `spring-refresh`, `http-probe`
- [x] Fingerprint and `mnemo-warmup.manifest.json` (includes cache type)
- [x] `mnemo-warmup bench`: 3 cold starts, none vs AppCDS vs AOT, Markdown savings table

### Phase 2: Kubernetes delivery (v0.2.0)
- [x] `mnemo-warmup fetch` (init container): look up by fingerprint, verify, copy to
      emptyDir; try AOT, then AppCDS, then give up cleanly
- [x] `mnemo-warmup run` (entrypoint): validate manifest, add archive flag or fall back
- [x] Archive store backend (open decision 1), including upload from trainer
- [x] Container image (tools image, see `docs/adr/0004-tools-image.md`)
- [x] Trainer CronJob, `train` command with a Lease, Helm chart with `cacheType` value (`docs/adr/0005-trainer-and-chart.md`)
- [x] Example Spring Boot app, tested on kind with JDK 21 (AppCDS) and JDK 25 (AOT) (`examples/`, `scripts/e2e-kind.sh`)

### Phase 2.5: simpler workload adoption (v0.2.5)
- [x] Offline injector: annotate a Deployment, preview, deploy through a Helm post-renderer (`docs/adr/0007-offline-injection-contract.md`, `docs/offline-injector.md`)
- [x] Shell-free native launcher, so distroless images work (`launcher/`, ADR 0004 amended)
- [x] Registry login providers and Amazon ECR through EKS workload identity (`docs/adr/0008-registry-auth-providers.md`, `docs/aws-workload-identity.md`)
- [x] Conservative retention guidance, no deletion (`docs/archive-retention.md`)
- [x] End-to-end check of the annotated path on kind with a distroless image, in CI on amd64 and arm64 (`scripts/e2e-kind-inject.sh`)
- [x] Adoption guide and configuration reference (`docs/configuration.md`, `docs/registry-auth.md`, `docs/operations.md`)
- [ ] Not verified yet: a live EKS and ECR, Helm 4, JDK 25 through the injector

### Phase 3: automation and ecosystem (v0.3.0)
- [x] Publish `warmup-core` to Maven Central so warden can depend on it (0.1.0, 0.2.0)
- [ ] Investigate which JVM flags invalidate an archive (e.g. `SoftMaxHeapSize` vs `-Xmx`)
      and support multi-profile archives accordingly
- [ ] Warden integration (implemented in the warden repo): inject the init container
- [ ] Savings metrics exported (startup ms, RSS) for dashboards
- [ ] Evidence (done so far: three application profiles at 1 CPU, `benchmarks/README.md`): Spring Boot gains, Jenkins is at parity, SonarQube (multi-process launcher) gains nothing
  - [ ] JDK 21 AppCDS vs JDK 25 Leyden AOT: speed, archive size on disk and over the network (#71)
  - [ ] Application size break-even: about 40 MB, 150 MB and 350 MB+ of JARs (#72)
  - [ ] HPA scale-out burst, 1 to 10 replicas, against a remote registry (#73)
  - [ ] Comparison matrix against vanilla JVM, build-time AppCDS/AOT and GraalVM Native Image (#74)
- [ ] Image-volume tools delivery consolidated for the beta: default, fallback, `pull-secret`, CI, more benchmarks (#76, ADR 0012)
- [ ] Warn in the preview when the image already carries a build-time cache (#70)
- [ ] Multi-JVM applications such as SonarQube: archives for child JVMs, or a documented limit (#77)
- [ ] Lighter install than extracting the tools image: curl script, Homebrew tap, asdf (#75)
- [ ] JDK 24 two-step AOT flow, only if users ask

### Later
- [ ] Optional build-time integrations (Gradle, GitHub Action) for non-Kubernetes users

## Decisions made
- Maven multi-module, `--release 21`, tested on JDK 25.
- Base package `io.github.baokhang83.mnemo.warmup`; picocli in the CLI module only.
- Java for all components (warden is Java too); no controller or webhook in this repo.
- Start with the standalone Helm chart; workload injection is done by warden.
- Maven coordinates aligned with warden: groupId `io.github.baokhang83.mnemo`.
- AOT from JDK 25 (single-step flags verified on 25.0.1); AppCDS for 21-24.

## Risks
- The JDK and Spring Boot are making this easier natively (JEP 514 already simplified the
  flags in 25); keep the value in cluster-aware sharing, fingerprinting and safe
  fallback, not in wrapping flags.
- Archive size and storage cost (AOT caches are larger than CDS archives).
- AppCDS behaviour on JDK 21-24 is verified (`docs/appcds-jdk-matrix.md`); the fingerprint
  rules (issue #20) are not yet measured with a real application.
- Market is unproven; validate with a few JVM platform teams before the warden integration.
